descriptionText: The inflection used to put neuter nouns into the subjective case (SD/430), used either as a suffix (for weak-nouns) or augmenting the last vowel (for strong-nouns). See the entry on the case for further details.

A pronominal prefix, most likely the neuter singular pronoun it, appearing in the word ayadda [it] went in the sentence the road west [it] once went straight (SD/247). See the entry on for more discussion.

An element in the name , whose Quenya equivalent seems to mean *World Tower (UT/222). Since the last element of this name is pillar, it is possible that the first element means world. This first element could be *abat, but it could also be *aban with the last n becoming t according to the Adunaic rules for , as suggested before by several authors (/9, /BAN1). Andreas Moehn further suggested () it may have replaced earlier Earth, though the two words could also co-exist with slightly different meanings.

A noun translated as “strength, endurance, fidelity”, and used as an example of noun declension in Lowdham’s Report (SD/431). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/9) that it may be related to the Elvish root ᴹ√ “endure”. It may also be related to the name “*Steadfast, Faithful”.
conceptualDevelopment: This word also appeared in earlier Adûnaic names and (both glossed “Land of Gift”), where it apparently had the meaning “gift”. These names were eventually replaced by in which the element means “gift”, freeing abâr to have the meaning: “strength, endurance, fidelity”.

descriptionText: The Adunaic name of the Tar-, the 19th rulers of Numenor (UT/222). His Quenya name appears to mean *World Tower. The last element of his Adunaic name is clearly Ad. pillar, so perhaps its meaning is similar. If so, the first element of his Adunaic name may mean World. Andreas Moehn suggested (/BAN1) this element is likely * or aban, with the final n altered to t in the compound according to the rules of Adunaic .

The Adunaic name that Lowdham used to address Jeremy in Tolkiens unfinished story: The Notion Club Papers (SD/252). In an earlier version of the story, Jeremy was called MQ. (SD/290) and Abrazan may be the Adunaic equivalent of that name, meaning Steadfast, Faithful. If so, its first element is probably related to Ad. strength, endurance, fidelity. Andreas Moehn suggested (/BAR) that the entire name may be the of an unattested verb *abraza- to stand fast.

A prepositional suffix variously translated as (in)to or (to)ward, and in one place against (SD/247, SD/429). It can appears as either -ada or -ad (SD/429), but in most examples it is -ada, the one exception being Starwards.

A noun meaning west(ward) (SD/435, PE17/18). Tolkien stated that was a loan word from Eldarin speech in the language of the Folk of Hador, from which Numenorean was later derived (PE17/18). Probably it is derived from S. west, as suggested by several authors (/9, /NDU). Tolkien stated that it was an adjective and its proper noun form was (SD/435), but adun was used as a noun in phrases such as Barim an-adun Lords of the West (SD/247).

The Adunaic word for the Numenoreans themselves, clearly related to west (PE17/18, SD/240). It is attested only in plural forms Adunai (normal plural) and Adunaim (subjective plural). The final vowel of its singular form must be a long a; if it were short, its plural form would be **Aduni instead of the attested Adunai.

Son of Ar- and the 20th ruler of Numenor, whose Quenya name was . In both languages, his name (somewhat heretically) means Lord of the West (LotR/1036, S/267). Its first element means west, which implies that its second element means lord, but it isnt clear whether this element is *akhor or *. I think that khor is more likely, because it resembles the Primitive Elvish root rule, govern, possess, to which it may be related.

The language of Numenor, appearing in a 1965 document first published in Nature of Middle-earth in 2021 (NM/323). Prior to that point, various hypothetical words have been proposed for this languages name, such as *Adunaiye (Andreas Moehn, ), *Adunaye (Thorsten Renk, /1), and Adunaiye (my own invention), modelled after Elvish.
According to Tolkien, this is the proper noun form of the adjective west (SD/435), though adun is used as a noun in some examples as well.

englishWord: [the] road west once went straight, (lit.) west straight road once went
descriptionText:
The 11th phrase of the (SD/247), whose word order varied considerably in the different drafts of the text. The first two words are the adjectives west and straight, right, true. They modify the subject road, path, way, which is in the rather than the . This is consistent with the grammatical rules of Lowdhams Report, since the verb ayadda has a pronominal suffix a- *it (SD/429).

The fourth word is an adverb once, then. The verb form yadda seems to be the tense of # to go, functioning here as a pluperfect (see SD/439). This makes sense in the narrative, since this sentence describes the previous state (the road west going straight to Valinor) while the next sentence uses the aorist tense to describe the current state (all roads being bent around the now-round world).

Tolkiens glosses match the word order of the Adunaic sentence: west straight road once went. This might be rendered in more ordinary English as [the] road west once went straight.

The previous (second draft) version of this sentence had more differences from the final version than any other sentence in the second draft (SD/312). It had a different word order, with the adjective straight appearing directly before the verb, perhaps functioning as an adverb. It has eluk instead of and the verb form yadda is missing the pronominal prefix a-. Unfortunately, Christopher Tolkien did not publish the English glosses for this sentence, so it is hard to decipher the meaning (if any) of these differences.

The first draft of the 11th phrase of the (SD/312). It resembles the final version, but is missing the adverb and has the verb to lie instead of to go.

The first two words adun west and batan road are the same as in the final version. The verb form akhaini lay seems to be the tense of the verb # to lie. The word ezendi straight (instead of later ) appears at the end, perhaps functioning as an adverb.
The masculine personification of death (SD/426). This could be the Adunaic name for .
A noun for death attested both as an independent word (SD/426) and in the compound agannalo death-shadow (SD/247).

The 9th phrase of the (SD/247). The subject agannalo death-shadow is a compound of death and shadow in the case. The next word heavy is simply an adjective, and nenud on us is a combination of the pronoun us and the prepositional suffix on. Since there is no verb, the subjective here functions as the verb to be (SD/429), so that the English translation should be the death-shadow is heavy on us, though Tolkien did not include is in his translation.

In the previous (second draft) version of this sentence, the spelling of some words were slightly different: buruda (as it was in the first draft) instead of the final form buroda and nenu instead of the final form nenud (SD/312). The first draft of this sentence uses the same words but is grammatically different.

The first draft of the 9th phrase of the (SD/312), which was close to the final version but had minor differences in spelling and grammar. The subject agannulo death-shade seems to be in the rather than the , and nulo shade is a variant spelling of later . The word burudan heavy seems to buruda (so spelled in the second draft but in the final version) with the predicate suffix is. The final word nenum on us is a combination of the pronoun us and the prepositional suffix -num on (nenu in the second draft and nenud in the final version).

The Adunaic name of the river S. Greyflood (UT/263), also glossed flood under shadow (VT42/9). This later name does not fit the Adunaic phonetic rules described by Tolkien in Lowdhams Report, since sh [] is not a phoneme used in Adunaic (SD/418). It may be that Tolkien changed his mind about the phonemes of Adunaic, or it may be that Agathurush had already undergone some of the phonetic changes leading to the Westron language, which had this sound (LotR/1120). It isnt clear how this name could be decomposed into its elements.
An element of the name that might be a noun meaning glory; see the entry for that name for further discussion.

An earlier name for the ship , likely the Adunaic equivalent of that name (SD/372, PM/156). Aglarrama was glossed Castle of the Sea, but many students of Tolkiens languages feel that this is unlikely to be a literal translation of the name. The first part of its Quenya name is Q. glory, and the element Ad. of its Adunaic name may have the same meaning, possibly as a loan word from S. . It is not clear what the last element of the name would mean. This analysis is all rather speculative, since it isnt even clear what languages the names Aglarrama and Alcarondas belong to.

A suffix in the word far away, a derivative of far (SD/247). Some authors have suggested that -ak is an intensive suffix very instead of suffix meaning away (, /32). However, the corresponding Quenya word far away is a combination (away) from and far, so it seems to me that the literal translation away is more likely to be correct (this translation of va was published after and were written).

The Adunaic name of Numenor after its fall, the equivalent of Q. (S/281). Tolkien usually translated this word as Downfallen, but its literal meaning was (She) That Has Fallen (PE17/111, SD/247). The final element seems to be a feminine suffix, also seen in . The middle element -kallab- seems to be the past formation kallaba of the verb to fall (down). The function of the initial a- isnt clear, but it may be some sort of perfective augment, as seen in the Quenya tense; see the discussion of the Adunaic for more information.

Other Interpretations: Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/36) that the prefix a- is probably some kind of emphatic suffix rather than evidence of another verb tense. Thorsten Renk proposes (/39) that the a- is a relative pronoun that, analogous to Q. , which is an interesting possibility.
A noun for chasm attested only in the prepositional phrase akhasada into chasm (SD/247) and akhas-ada chasm-into (SD/311), the latter example making it clear which element means what.

The Adûnaic name of (SD/376). According to Christopher Tolkien, the invention of this Adûnaic name preceded the use of Q. as the name of the Blessed Realm, and was likely the inspiration for this Quenya name (SD/376). The later status of Ad. Amân as the name of Manwë is unclear, but it could be that the ancestors of the Númeróreans conflated the name of the Valar with the name of the land he ruled.
conceptualDevelopment: The first Adûnaic name for Manwë was (SD/55).

descriptionText: A draft version of the Adunaic name for , later replaced by (SD/376).

The primitive form of , the Adunaic name of Manwe, written in allcaps as AMAN (SD/420). Usually Tolkien used capitalization for primitive roots, but in this case it is more like to be a form derived from an unattested Primitive Adunaic root *MAN, probably related to the Primitive Elvish root M.

The Adûnaic name for the Blessed Realm, home of the Valar (SD/388, SD/420). Its Quenya equivalent would be , though Tolkien did not coin the Quenya name until a later conceptual stage of his legendarium. The Adûnaic word is derived from their name for the ruler of the Bless Realm: (Manwë). Its literal meaning is “Manwë’s Land”.
conceptualDevelopment: The first Adûnaic name for the Blessed Realm was (SD/385).

descriptionText: A draft Adunaic name for the Blessed Realm, later replaced by (SD/385). Its initial element is a draft name for land also seen in the draft name Land of Gift. Its final element is , the Adunaic name of Manwe, joined to the first element with an elided form of the genitive prefix of. Therefore, the literal meaning of the name is Land of Aman (Manwe).

A noun for mother (SD/434). Tolkien gave two forms of this word, ammi and amme, with no indication as to which would be preferred. However, ammi resembles a plural word, and Tolkien elsewhere stated that such forms tended to change their final vowel to -e (SD/438), so my guess is that ammi is an archaic form. This word is probably related to the Elvish root mother. Some authors have suggested it is directly related to MQ. (/10, /Adunaic), but as Andreas Moehn points out (/MAM) such basic words are rarely borrowed from other languages, so the relationship is more likely from the Primitive Elvish root.
The suffix for singular , reduced to -n when the noun ends in a vowel (SD/430, 436).
An apparent primitive form of the Classical Adunaic agental suffix , attested in the Primitive Adunaic word = + -an (SD/421).

A prefix translated as of (SD/247) and one of the ways that relationships are expressed in Adunaic (SD/429). According to Tolkien, it is not a preposition ... it is the equivalent of an inflexion or suffix (SD/435). As such, it is used to form adjectives from nouns, as western, *of the West from the West. When following another noun, it is often elided so that the a is lost, as in King of the Numenoreans (SD/429) and Bar nAnadune Lord of Numenor (SD/428). This elision occurs in most examples, but seems not to happen in some cases:

  • When the an- is separated from the modified noun: balik hazad an-Nimruzir ships seven of-Nimruzir (SD/247).
  • When the modified nouns is declined into the subjective case: Barim an-Adun Lords of the West (SD/247).
  • However, when the subjective noun ends in a vowel, elision still occurs: narika nBari nAdun Eagles of the Lords of the West (SD/251).

Tolkien used a dash to separate an- from the noun to which it is prefixed but omitted the dash when the prefix was elided. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/10) that Ad. an- may be related to the Sindarin genitive marker S. with, by

A suffix that appears in some adjectives, and may be used to form a in Adunaic, that is an adjective formed from a verb. Helge Fauskanger suggested (/Adunaic) that it may be a cognate of Q. , derived from Primitive Elvish . There are two examples: beloved to love and humbled * to humble. Both cases seem to be passive participles (also called past participles in English grammar), describing a noun that is the object of the verbal action: that which is loved, that which is humbled.

Unlike other Adunaic , these participle forms appear after the noun they modify instead of before. See the entry on the for further discussion.

A suffix that is used in some examples for : creating nouns from verbs that indicate the agent who performs the verbs action. The clearest example is wise man derived (after some ancient sound modifications) from to understand. This formation means *one who understands. Less clear examples are * wright, *builder, perhaps from a verb * to build, and conquerer, perhaps a combined of all and a verb ? to take, meaning *one who takes all.

It is not clear how this suffix related to the similar suffix used for form adjectives from verbs. See the entry on for further discussion. Andreas Moehn suggested (/TAN) that -an as an agental formation may be related to human being.

A noun translated human being (SD/426) given as an example of a noun ending in a long vowel that (archaically) uses the declension for a (SD/437), an example of the extremely rare class of Strong-IIb nouns. By the time of Classical Adunaic, it could be declined as an ordinary instead. It also had masculine and feminine variants anu (human) man and ani (human) woman (SD/434) but in ordinary speech it seems likely that more specific words would be used: man, male, female, woman.

The Adunaic name for Numenor (Q. ), with the same meaning as its Quenya name: Westernesse (S/261). In The Silmarillion appendix, Christopher Tolkien stated that is it a loan word from Elvish (SA/andune). According to J.R.R. Tolkiens own writing (SD/426), this is true, albeit not directly. Anadune is a feminized form of the adjective western, of the west, which is itself related to S. west.

The 6th phrase of the (SD/247). Its subject Numenor is in the rather than the . This is consistent with the grammatical rules of Lowdhams Report, which allowed a normal subject if the verb has a pronominal inflection (SD/429), in this case the prefix hi- she of the verb hikalba (place names in Adunaic are often ).

The placement of the adjective beloved after the noun is curious, since according to Tolkien adjectives normally precede the nouns they modify (SD/428). Perhaps in this instance the adjective is used as a noun. Its manuscript gloss the beloved instead of simply beloved (as in the typescript) supports this possibility. Alternately, it could be in an abnormal position because it is a (verbal adjective).

The verbs in the typescript and manuscript versions are slightly different: kallaba fell down (SD/247) and kalba fell (VT24/12), the and tenses of the verb to fall (down). Tolkien also vacillated between these two forms in the second draft version of the sentence before settling on the aorist. Since the fall of Numenor had already come to pass in the fictional context of the Lament, the past tense here could be functioning here as a pluperfect (SD/439), but the aorist tense would also work if the sentence describes the fall of Numenor at that point in the narrative. Tolkiens vacillation is therefore understandable: either verb form could work albeit with slightly different meanings. The Quenya translation of this sentence, MQ. (SD/247), uses the simple past instead of the perfect, matching the Adunaic manuscript version rather than typescript.

The first draft of the 6th phrase of the (SD/311). It differs from the final version in its grammar and in the omission of the word beloved. The subject anaduni seems to be an earlier version of Numenor. The verb akallabi fell in ruin is an early form of to fall (down), perhaps in the tense.

An adjective translated western formed from the noun the West which was in turn formed from the adjective west; the initial was the genitival prefix (SD/435). This adjective anaduni was in turn femininized to produce the place name Westeresse, Numenor.
An element of the name (SD/389), possibly meaning bliss; see the entry for that name for further discussion.

The Adûnaic name for Q. (SD/389). The last element of this name is an for the verb “to love”, also seen in the name of his son “Elf-friend” (Q. ). The initial element seems to be the form of a noun , whose meaning is unclear. The equivalent element in his Quenya name is “Blessed Realm”, but Tolkien had not yet coined this word when he invented the name Aphanuzîr. Andreas Moehn suggested (/PHAN) that it means “bliss”. This fits the earlier story of the Lost Road (LR), in which Tolkien wrote of various incarnations of a father and son whose names were “Bliss-friend” and “Elf-friend” in many languages. Amandil and Elendil were two of these incarnations.
conceptualDevelopment: The first Adûnaic name given to this character was (SD/365).

descriptionText: A prefix appearing before the Adûnaic names of kings and queens, the equivalent of Q. Tar- “High” (SA/ar(a)). It is most likely either a prefixal form of Ad. “king” or derived from the same root.
conceptualDevelopment: This prefix was introduced in the earliest versions of Adûnaic from the 1940s (SD/311, SD/248), and survived in the later Adûnaic names of The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion.

descriptionText: The Adunaic name for the capital of Numenor, whose Quenya name is (SD/363, PM/145). The final element seems to be a feminizing suffix, also seen in Ad. . The initial element is the same as that used in the name of kings and queens, and the middle element means heaven, so perhaps the literal meaning is something like *Royal Heaven (City), similar in the sense to the Quenya name.
A short phrase illustrating the Adunaic compositional (SD/435).

A phrase given by Tolkien as an example of how a pair of nouns would be declined into the case, with only the last noun inflected (SD/429). The entire noun phrase would be the subject of the sentence. It is contrasted with , where the first noun is inflected instead. This would be a the sentences Ar-Pharazon (is) a conquerer.

The 3rd phrase of the (SD/247). It differed from its earlier drafts only in its use of grammar. Tolkiens gloss was was warring against Powers, omitting the name Ar-Pharazon because Lowdham was unsure how to translate it. In more ordinary English might be Ar-Pharazon was warring against the Powers.

The subject Ar-Pharazonun is the form of the name Ar-. The verb azaggara was warring is a form of to wage war, either the past tense or continuative-past tense (see the entry for that tense for further discussion). The last word Avaloiyada against the Powers is the plural form of Power, God with the prepositional suffix toward, against separated from the i of the plural by the usual y.

The previous (second draft) version of this sentence differs from the final version in two ways (SD/312). First, the subject is in the instead of the case, perhaps because Tolkien had not finalized the rules for the subjective case. Second, its verb form was azagrara, although the final verb form azaggara was written nearby as an alternative. See the verb for possible interpretations.

The first draft of the 3rd phrase of the (SD/311). It differs from the final version primarily in grammar. It has a difficult-to-interpret form azgaranadu of the verb . See the entry to that verb for possible interpretations. The last word avaloi-si seems to be the plural form of Power, God, changed from the plural form avaloi-men.

englishWord: King Pharazon is Lord of Anadune
descriptionText: An example sentence illustrating Adunaic grammar: it is a copula (a to be expression) without an explicit verb for is (SD/428). The subject of the sentence, Ar-Pharazonun, is in the case, which represents the verb to be. The rest of the sentence, Bar nAnadune Lord of Anadune (Numenor) is the predicate and is in the . This sentence also provides an example of the use of the genitive prefix of, here elided to n because of the preceding uninflected noun.

A phrase given by Tolkien as an example of how the case can be used to represent the verb to be (SD/429). Since the first noun the subject, the second noun is the predicate and the verb is is implied. Depending on context, the sentenced could refer to the past so that the subjective would represent was instead. This sentence is contrasted with , where the second noun is inflected in the subjective instead, so that the entire noun phrase would be the subject: King Ar-Pharazon the Conqueror....
A noun translated as king (SD/429). The Adunaic word for queen is not attested, but could be a feminized form of this word, such as *ari.

An Adunaic name for Morgoth, perhaps coined by Sauron when he introduced the worship of the dark god to the Numenoreans, translated as Lord (SD/376). It is derived from the word king and was sometimes used in a compound together with Morgoths true Adunaic name: Arun- (SD/367). In other writings (SD/357) it was the original Adunaic name of Morgoth before he fell to evil, but that hardly makes sense in the conceptual scenario of the later Silmarillion, in which Morgoth had already become evil before men awoke.

A rejected draft version of the Adunaic name for Morgoth translated Lord, replaced by of the same meaning (SD/376). It is transparently a derivative of the Elvish root M, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/18). A later form of this word, * lord, may appears as an element in the name Lord of the West.

An phrase illustrating Adunaic grammar, in particular how the genitive prefix of must be used when a plural noun needs to be put into a genitive relationship with another noun (SD/429). Without the an-, the preceding noun would be in an relationship instead. Here the an- is elided to n because of the preceding uninflected noun.

An otherwise unexplained root Tolkien gave to illustrate a pronunciation example (SD/421). It may not be a real root. If it is real, it is either a <a l="pad" v="biconsonantal-root"/> with <a l="pad" v="vowel-prefixion"/> or a <a l="pad" v="triconsonantal-root"/> with a lost initial consonant such as <a l="pad" v="[]"/> or <a l="pad" v="[]"/>.
A word Tolkien used to illustrate Adunaic pronunciation (pronounced [azdi]) without giving its meaning (SD/421).

The suffix for in Adunaic, with the a lengthened to a in duals (SD/428-430). In later (Exilic?) Adunaic, the a was long in all cases (SD/431). See the entry on for further details. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/11) that -at is derived from the same Primitive Elvish form as the Quenya dual.

A noun for father (SD/434). Tolkien gave two forms of this word, attu and atto, with no indication as to which would be preferred. For reasons similar to those given in the entry for mother, my guess is that attu is an archaic form, and atto was preferred by the time of Classical Adunaic. This word is probably related to the Elvish root father, perhaps from Primitive Elvish M.
The feminine form of God, Power, translated Goddess (SD/428). Like its masculine equivalent, it is probably pronounced [awale], since the sound in Adunaic was sometime written v (SD/434).

The Adûnaic name for , though it may also (or instead) have referred the Blessed Realm, home of the Valar (SD/241). It was translated “Haven of the Gods” (SD/361). Given its meaning, the name seems to contain the word Ad. , the Adûnaic name for the Valar. It seems likely that Ad. Avallôni is direct borrowing of Q. “Outer Isle”, reinterpreted by the Númenorieans to fit their language. It is probably pronounced [awallōni], since the sound in Adûnaic was sometime written “v” (SD/434).
conceptualDevelopment: An earlier form of this name, Avallondē may have been a mixed name, containing the Quenya element ᴹQ. (SD/344).

descriptionText: An Adûnaic noun translated as “God” or “Power” (SD/247, 305), the equivalent of (and possibly derived from) Q. . It is probably pronounced [awalō], since the sound in Adûnaic was sometime written “v” (SD/434). It frequently appeared in its plural or subjective plural forms Avalôi(m) “Powers, Gods”.
conceptualDevelopment: In early drafts of Adûnaic its plural was Avalâi with a long â instead of ô, perhaps indicating an earlier singular form Avalâ closer to Vala. Earlier still this word was given as plural Balāi, a more direct derivative of the Elvish root form ᴹ√.

descriptionText: An earlier version of the Adunaic word for Q. (SD/344), later replaced by Avalai >> Avaloi. It is only attested in its plural form Balai.

An Adunaic name for a goddess with the title Star-kindler (SD/428). Though Tolkien never made it explicit, it is clearly the Adunaic name of (S. ). This name is curious, since [v] is not one of the phonemes used in Adunaic (SD/418). Most likely it is pronounced [awradi]. Tolkien said that to represent the sound , he sometimes used v in the Anglicanizing of Adunaic names (SD/434). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/12) that it may be a derivative of Primitive Elvish .

A hypothetical noun for war appearing as an element in the verb to wage war, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/24), though as others have suggested (/Adunaic, /ZAGR) it could equally well be azgar.

A verb meaning to wage war (SD/439), one of two examples of an and the only one with any attested inflections. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne initially suggested it is composed of the words * war and a causative suffix * (/24), but later suggested (/12) it may be related * so that its literal meaning was *wield a weapon or *put to the sword, similar to MQ. wield a weapon, fight < M sword. Andreas Moehn also suggested (/ZAGR) the verb may be related to * sword.

This verb appears in slightly different forms in each version of the , changing as follows: azgaranadu (SD/311) >> azagrara (SD/312) >> azaggara (SD/247). All three versions have similar glosses, was waging war or was warring, which seems to imply these are all instances of the tense. As they are the only clear instances of this tense, it is difficult to decipher the conceptual development of this verb.

The first form azgaranadu belongs to the draft Adunaic period and is probably grammatically distinct from the later forms. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne thoroughly analyzed this draft form (/35). The two later forms appeared in very similar versions of the Lament. Rather than representing a revision of the grammar, they could represent distinct verb tenses, as for example Tolkiens vacillation between the forms hikalba and hikallaba in the sentence . The question is, to which tense does each form belong?

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/28) concluded that the azaggara represents the without analyzing azagrara. Andreas Moehn agreed with them in his grammatical article on Adunaic () but changed his mind in his etymological analysis (/ZAGR), concluding it is the past tense instead. I also believe azaggara is more likely to be a simple past tense.

The double-g of the form azaggara resembles other verb forms identified as the tense in the theories used here, and it seems likelier to me that Tolkien changed the verb from the continuative-past to the simple past without revising the gloss. The second a in azaggara is likely inserted in the verb stem to break up the consonant cluster in az-ggara, since Adunaic allows at most two consecutive (SD/418).

If the above reasoning is correct, this would make the form azagrara the best candidate for the continuative-past. Perhaps the repetition of the final suffix -ra is used to mark the continuous nature of the action. All of this is highly speculative, however, since we are working only from a single example.
The Adunaic word for sea (SD/429), appearing as azar in some early texts (SD/305). It is fully declined on SD/431.
A draft word for sea, deleted and replaced with azar (SD/305), which later become . This word reappeared later with a different meaning: gold.
A noun given as an example of a <a l="ad" v="genitive"/> compound (SD/429), translated sea-lands, maritime regions (SD/435) but literally meaning *lands of the sea.

englishWord: that [the] seas should gush into [the] chasm
descriptionText:
The 5th phrase of the (SD/247). The subject azriya is the plural of sea. Judging by the glosses, the verbal prefix most likely indicates the or moods (see those entries for discussion). The verb form phursa resembles the tense of the verb , except that the long a is unusual. Perhaps this variation is because the verb is actually in an infinitive form, though Andreas Moehn instead suggested the verb stem may be a derived verb *phursa- (/PHUR). The last word akhasada is the word chasm with the prepositional suffix towards, into.

The gloss of the manuscript version was that seas should gush into Chasm (VT24/12). This gloss seems to indicate that this sentence might actually be a subordinate phrase of the preceding sentence Lords of the West, they broke the Earth with assent from Eru. This would fit well with its use of the optative/subjunctive mood, so that this phrase gives reason why the Valar broke the Earth (to sink Numenor). However, both the manuscript and typescript versions separated the two sentences with an ellipsis ..., indicating that they are separate sentences.

The first draft of the 5th phrase of the (SD/311). Its has the same vocabulary as the final version except that it has might (an adverb?) instead of the prefix . This nai is almost certainly a variant of Q. maybe, be it that.

The draft version has several other grammatical differences from later versions. The subject azre seas seems to be a simple rather than plural. Tolkien initially wrote phurusam for the verb and then changed to phurrusim flow, perhaps and tenses of the verb , respectively. Both conjugations have the plural verb suffix . The last phrase akhas-ada into Chasm is essentially identical to the final version, however.

The Adûnaic name of Q. , having a similar meaning “Friend of the Sea” (SD/359). The first element is the form of “sea” and the second is an for the verb stem (PM/373). An earlier version of this name, Azrabêl, predates Tolkien’s invention the objective case for Adûnaic (SD/359).
conceptualDevelopment: The first Adûnaic name given to this character was (SD/305).

descriptionText: The first version of the Adunaic name of Q. (SD/305), quickly rejected and replaced by Azrabel, later . Its rejected elements have the same meaning as Azrubel. Interestingly, the suffix -zir -lover reappeared in the later names and , though as derivations of instead of iri-. The word also reappeared later with the meaning gold.
A noun for east attested only in the prepositional phrase azulada eastward, *to the east = azul + to(ward) (SD/247, 312).

A particle glossed dont in the phrase Dont touch me!. It may be a derivative of the Elvish root M refuse, deny, say no, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (/Adunaic). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/25, /13) it is an example of the mood mentioned by Tolkien SD/439, where optative is an expression of a desire or wish. If so, it expresses a negative wish. A positive wish might be expressed by the particle .

An isolated Adunaic sentences appearing in The Notion Club Papers (SD/250). None of its elements appear elsewhere, making it difficult to interpret, but there is a some consensus in the literature as to the likeliest interpretations. The first word, dont could be derived from the Primitive Elvish root refuse, deny, possibly an example of the mood (, ). The first element of the second word could be a pronoun ki- you. The middle portion tabda could be the aorist form of a verb * touch. The last element -he seems to be the object pronoun me, though Thorsten Renk (/18) suggested it is an imperative marker instead.

The noun for ship, attested only in the plural (balik) and objective (balku) forms (SD/247, PM/151). Its plural form indicates that it is a (Strong I), so its final vowel must be short. In theory its final vowel could be any of a, i or u, each of which would be replaced by long i in . However, its attested form uses the variant objective-with-syncope form balku instead of ordinary *baluk. Since the Adunaic seems only to occur for nouns with two identical short vowels, this indicates the singular form of this word is balak.

The 8th phrase of the (SD/247). As written, it seems to be an incomplete noun phrase rather then a full sentence. It contains neither a verb nor a noun in the case that could represent a copula (to be statement).

The first word, balik ships is the normal plural of # ship. It is in a composition with the number seven, a construction discussed on SD/428, literally meaning *seven of ships. This is modified by the phrase an-Nimruzir of Elendil consisting of the genitive prefix of and the name (Q. ). The final word, azulada eastward(s) is a composition of east and the suffix (to)wards.

The final typescript and manuscript versions differ only in that the manuscript is missing the dash - in the genitive an-Nimruzir of Elendil (VT24/12). The previous (second draft) version of the phrase is missing the entire prefix an- (SD/312). The first draft had a rather different sentence.

The first draft of the 8th phrase of the (SD/312), which is essentially a different sentence from the final version. The first word Adunaim is the subjective plural of Numenorean. The second word, azulada eastwards is the same as in the final version: a composition of east and the suffix (to)wards.

The 12th ruler of Numenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- Shipbuilder, Shipwright (PM/151). The first element of his name is the form of ship. Therefore, the second element most likely means wright, *builder. This name appears only in a draft list of the kings of Numenor from the early 1950s, and falls between the conceptual periods of Middle Adunaic and Late Adunaic in the terminology used here.

The noun for wife, given as an example of a noun with a long vowel in its final syllable that (archaically) uses the declension for a (SD/437), an example of the rare class of Strong-Ib nouns. By the time of Classical Adunaic, it could be declined as an ordinary instead.

A noun translated as “lord” (SD/311, 428). This nouns wins the prize for “most inflected Adûnaic noun”, since we have declensions for this noun in both the draft Adûnaic grammar and the later grammar of Lowdham’s Report. As such, it is very helpful for comparing how the noun declensions changed as Tolkien developed Adûnaic grammar. For example, comparing its draft plurals bāri/bārim to its later plural bârî/bârîm indicate the draft plural was originally formed with a short rather than long i. There are a few lingering examples of this short-i plural in later writings (SD/247, 251).
conceptualDevelopment: In earlier writings the rejected name “Lord” (SD/376) indicates a possible earlier form of this noun; Kherû itself was changed to . A similar form reappears in later writings in the name “Lord of the West”: either akhôr or “lord”. Whether or not this later word replaced bâr is unknown.

englishWord: Lords of [the] West, they rent [the] Earth with assent from Eru
translatedWord: Bârim an-Adûn yurahtam dâira sâibêth-mâ Êruvô
transliteratedWord: Bârim an-Adûn yurahtam dâira sâibêth-mâ Êruvô
pronunciationText: Bârim an-Adûn yurahtam dâira sâibêth-mâ Êruvô
descriptionText:
The 4th phrase of the (SD/247). One major conceptual change from earlier versions was that the subject of the sentence was plural Barim an-Adun (Lords of the West) instead of the earlier singular Barun an-Adun (Lord of the West). It seems that Tolkien decided that the drowning of Numenor was attributed to all of the Valar rather than just Manwe. A similar change from singular to plural was made in the corresponding Quenya sentence: herunumen >> numeheruvi.

The subject Barim of this sentence is the plural of lord. It is modified by the adjectival phrase an-Adun of the West, with the genitive prefix of added to the noun . The verb has the 3rd-plural suffix yu- they. In the grammatical rules of Lowdhams Report this makes the subject emphatic, with a meaning more like It was the Lords of the West who broke the Earth... (SD/429).

The verb form rahtam is the tense of to break with the verb plural suffix . The object of the sentence, Earth, is in the .

The base sentence is modified by the prepositional phrase saibeth-ma Eruvo with assent from Eru. The combination saibeth-ma is the word assent and the prepositional suffix with. The final word Eruvo is the name and the prepositional suffix of, with the usual (which was sometimes written v as mentioned on SD/434) between the u and the following suffix.

englishWord: the Lord of West broke asunder earth assent-with of God
descriptionText:
The first draft of the 4th phrase of the (SD/311). It differs considerably from the final version:

  • The subject is singular Lord rather than plural Lords, as is the case with the second draft as well.
  • The adjectival phrase aduno of the West uses the case instead of the later genitive prefix .
  • The verb form is rakkhatu, perhaps the draft tense of an early version rakhat- of the verb . It later changed >> urahhata >> urahta >> yurahta. It is glossed broke asunder rather than simply broke as in later versions.
  • The word for Earth is rather than later .
  • In the final phrase sobethuma eruvo assent-with of God, the two words are likely declined into the and cases, respectively.

An example sentence showing how the can sometimes be used for the subject of a sentence (SD/429). The subject is lord while the verb has the masculine singular pronoun prefix u- he. Such a prefix is required when the subject is in the normal case (SD/429). The verb form kallaba is the tense of to fall. This sentence is contrasted with in which the subject is in the case.

englishWord: the lord fell, it was the lord who fell
descriptionText: An example sentence showing how the case is used for the subject of sentences (SD/429). The subject barun lord is the subjective form of . The verb form kallaba is the tense of to fall. The masculine singular pronoun prefix u- he is optional, but when present makes the sentence emphatic: it was the lord who fell (SD/429). This sentence is contrasted with in which the subject is instead in the , which makes the pronoun u- required rather than optional (but not emphatic).
A hypothetical verb, perhaps meaning walk, that may appear as an element in the noun road, path, way.

A noun variously translated as road, path or way (SD/247, 431; VT24/12) and fully declined on SD/431. This noun also appears in the variant strong-plural form batin that was sometimes used with Weak I nouns in older and poetic writing (SD/247, 435). Its ordinary weak plural form batani appears in the declension chart on SD/431. Several authors have suggested (/13, /BAT) that this noun may be a derivative of the Elvish root M tread (Ety/BAT). If so, its final element may be the agental suffix , and its initial element may be a verb * walk, so that the literal sense of the word might be *walkway.

The noun for wind, attested only in the plural (bawib) and subjective plural (bawiba) forms (SD/247, SD/312). Its plural form indicates that it is a (Strong I), so its final vowel must be short, but in theory it could be any of a, i or u, each of which would be replaced by long i in . Nouns with identical vowels are more common, however, so *bawab is the most likely singular form, though as Helge Fauskanger points out (/Adunaic) the normal form could also be the weak noun *bawab with a poetic strong plural (SD/435).

The 7th phrase of the (SD/247). The subject bawiba is the plural of # wind. There is no verb, so the subjective here functions as the to-be verb were, as discussed on SD/429. The adjective dulgi is the plural of black, agreeing in number with the subject.

This sentence did not appear at all in the first draft. In the second draft of the Lament, it was simply the noun phrase dulgu bawib *black wind rather than a full sentence (SD/312). Curiously, the adjective in the second draft did not agree in number with the noun it modified.

This unglossed root appears only as an element in the name Friend of the Sea, Sea-lover (SD/305). It has a sense similar to that of Ad. love, desire. Perhaps it is distinct from Ad. ZIR in that it has more to do with friendship than desire. It could be distantly related to the elvish root , perhaps mel- > mbel- > bel- in the Avari tongue that influenced Primitive Adunaic, but this is purely speculative.

This root also contradicts statements by Tolkien elsewhere that Primitive Adunaic only had the vowels a, i and u. Perhaps it should be *BIL, as with Ad. say the primitive root of Ad. expression, saying, word.
A rejected Adunaic root attested as iri- and having to do with love (SD/305), perhaps related to the Primitive Elvish root M desirable, beautiful.

A verb stem bel- attested only in the explanations for the -bel in the name Friend of the Sea, Sea-lover (SD/305, PM/373). The form bel- violates Adunaic phonetic rules given in Lowdhams Report, which state that can only be a long vowel in Adunaic (SD/423). See the discussion of its root form Ad. for possible explanations. The Classical Adunaic verb form might be bel-, while bel- may instead be its most primitive (early Elvish?) form.

This verb seems to have a sense similar to that of to love, desire. Perhap it is distinct from zir- in that it has more to do with friendship than desire, so that the verb means *to befriend or *to love (as a friend).

A noun attested only in its plural form beni servants as an element in the term Servants of God (SD/341, 357). This noun resembles the Sindarin word person, especially in the Sindarin lenited form -ben. The Adunaic noun may be related, having undergone phonetic development similar to that discussed for Ad. word, so that ben is ultimately derived from Primitive Elvish person, which could be its archaic meaning. Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/BIN) that it is derived from a root *BIN, possibly related to Ed. Vassal, Servant.

A noun translated as expression, saying, word (SD/427). It is likely derived from the Primitive Adunaic root say (SD/416). This word is very similar to Sindarin word, especially in the Sindarin lenited form beth. The ancient development of the Adunaic word may have been similar to Sindarin, with Primitive Elvish root M > *PET > Ad. BITH, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (/Adunaic).
A root glossed say (SD/416), from which expression, saying, word is most likely derived. It may be related to the Primitive Elvish root ; see the entry on for further discussion.

A verbal form of Ad. expression, saying, word attested only as an as part of the noun true-sayer (SD/427); see that entry for further discussion of its phonetic development. As suggested by Thorsten Renk suggested (/24, 26), the verb stem is probably bith-, consistent with its primitive root Ad. . Since agental forms generally have a lengthened or fortified vowel, the verb stem bith- could have the fortified agental form -beth.
An adjective glossed “heavy” (SD/247) or “very heavy” (VT24/12).
conceptualDevelopment: It appeared as buruda in early Adûnaic writings (SD/312).

descriptionText: A possible causative verbal suffix in to overshadow, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/24). It may be related to Primitive Elvish causative suffix . Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne instead suggested (/24) it may be related to the Adunaic prepositional suffix to, toward.
A noun translated as “Earth” in the final version of the (SD/247). It may be related to S. “land”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/13).
conceptualDevelopment: In the , this noun appeared as (SD/311).

descriptionText: The noun for Earth in the first draft version of the Lament of Akallabeth (SD/311), later replaced by (SD/247). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/17) that it may be related to the Elvish root M soil, earth.

A preposition translated as under (SD/247, 311) or beneath (VT24/12). It appeared in the usual suffixal position in the final version of the , but appeared before the noun it modified in the first draft version.
A noun translated as gloom derived from the root (SD/423). It is an example of how primitive , thereby producing diphthongs.
The root from which gloom is derived (SD/423), perhaps with a similar meaning.

A Primitive Adunaic word glossed gloom (SD/423), the only attested example of a for a . Ordinarily such a form would not be possible, since final consonant clusters did not appear in Primitive Adunaic (SD/418, 426). It is possible that such forms were valid in the case of medial semi-vowels [w] and [j], however, since , thereby preventing a cluster from forming.

A noun attested as the isolated word dolgu, described as a word with the evil sense of night or dark (SD/306). It may be related to S. night and N. obscure, hidden, dusky, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/13). It is similar to the word black appearing in the and the two may be variations of the same word, but most authors have suggested (/13-14, /Adunaic, /DULG, /11, 24) that they are distinct words. In the phonetic rules in Lowdhams Report from this period, a short o cannot appear in an Adunaic (SD/423), so perhaps the proper form of this noun should be *dolgu.

A verbal prefix in the sentence and translated as either so-as (SD/247) or should (VT24/12). It almost certainly indicates some verb-mood. Most authors have suggested it indicates the mood based on its glosses (/25, , /Adunaic). I think it could also be the mood, since in the first draft versions of the sentence the word was nai, clearly related to Q. maybe, may it be that used for the expression of a wish. Since it appears in only a single example, we dont have enough information to be sure.

A verbal prefix in the first draft sentence azre nai phurrusim akhas-ada (SD/311), expressing either the or verbal mood. It almost certainly related to Q. maybe, may it be that used for the expression of a wish, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/20). In later versions of the , this word was changed to .

A verb glossed “fell” in the (SD/247), but it is clear from context that its meaning is different from the ordinary verb for “to fall”: . Perhaps the sense of dubud- is “to fall under the influence of [shadow]” or “to fall under the cover of [shadow]”. Between the second draft and the final version version of the poem, the verb form changed from dubbudam ( tense) to dubdam (), in both cases with the plural verbal suffix .

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/23) that dubud- may be related to the Elvish root ᴹ√ “loom, hang over oppressively”, which would fit well with the sense “to fall under the cover of”.
conceptualDevelopment: The draft form of the verb was udūbanim, which is difficult to analyze. It is missing a second d, so the draft verb may be a dū̆b- or perhaps a dūban-. Patrick Wynne and Carl Hostetter suggested (/35-36) that the initial u- may be a 3rd-person pronominal prefix, but I think it may instead be the vowel augment of a tense; see that entry for further discussion.

descriptionText: An adjective translated black (SD/247). It appears in its plural form dulgi black in the final version of the (SD/247) and in its singular form dulgu in the second draft of this text (SD/312). It may be related to S. dark and N. obscure, hidden, dusky, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/14). It is likely related to or a variant of black, dark.
An adjective (or adverb?) translated as far (SD/247, SD/312).
A combination of far and the suffix (SD/247, 312), which could either mean away or be some kind of intensifier. See the entry for for further discussion.

englishWord: far away now (is) the Land of Gift
descriptionText:
The 13th phrase of the (SD/247). The first word far away is an adverb or emphatic adjective; see the entry for for further discussion. The second word now is an adverb. The last word Land of Gift is one of the names for Numenor. There is no subjective noun or a verb, so this phrase is a fragment rather than a full sentence.

The typescript version (and all earlier versions) had idon now (is) instead of ido now. See the entry for for further discussion.

The first draft of the 13th phrase of the (SD/312). It differs from the final version mainly in its use of ephalek far away for later and akallabeth instead of later ( appears instead in the last sentence of the final version). Like the final typescript version but unlike the final manuscript version, it uses idon lo! now is instead of ido now. This is may be a combination of the adverb ido now and the predicate suffix is used elsewhere in the draft version.

The 14th (and final) phrase of the (VT24/12). The first two words far and far away are repeated adjectives (or adverbs), the second with the added suffix -ak. This suffix either means away or is some kind of emphatic marker; see the entry for further discussion. The third word now is an adverb. The last word The Downfallen is the Adunaic name for Numenor after its destruction. It is prefixed with the pronoun she, turning the name into a small sentence She that hath fallen.

The typescript version (and all earlier versions) had idon now (is) instead of ido now (SD/247, 312). See the entry for for further discussion.

englishWord: far far away is now the Land of Gift
descriptionText: The first draft of the 14th (and final) phrase of the (SD/312). It differs from the final version mainly in its use of ephalek far away for later and athanate Land of Gift instead of later . In the final version of the Lament, another word for Land of Gift () appears in the second-to-last sentence instead. Like the final typescript version but unlike the final manuscript version, is uses idon is now instead of ido now. This is likely a combination of the adverb ido now and the predicate suffix is used elsewhere in the draft version.

The Adunaic word for God (SD/432), the equivalent of Q. , though Tolkien had not yet coined that name. In the conceptual development of this name, Tolkien first invented it as an Adunaic word (SD/312), only later adding it to Quenya. In this revised scenario, it is likely that the Adunaic word was a loan word from Elvish. See Ad. for a similar development.
Another Adunaic title for the Valar, translated Servants of God (SD/357). Since is God, the second element must be beni servants, the plural of otherwise unattested servant

A title for the race of men as the children of “God” (SD/247). It is only attested in the plural Êruhîn (SD/311, 358) and subjective plural Êruhînim (SD/247-8) forms “Children of God”. The suffix seems to have been a general patronymic in Adûnaic used for lines of descent, also appearing in “*Line of Elros [son] of Earendil”.
conceptualDevelopment: This name first appeared as Eruhil(di) (SD/341, 399), probably incorporating ᴹQ. “men”. In these early appearances Tolkien may have conceived of this as a Quenya word before introducing its Adûnaic form Êruhîn. In its early appearances the latter name sometimes had a short initial E: Eruhîn (SD/358), possibly another transitional form resembling later Sindarin . In still later writings, Tolkien coined a Quenya word Q. of the similar meaning, encompassing both Men and Elves.

englishWord: [the Children of Eru] fell under shadow
descriptionText:
The 2nd phrase of the (SD/247). Tolkien did not interpret the name Eruhinim in any version of the text, but elsewhere it is glossed Children of God (Eru) (SD/248). Tolkiens gloss was fell shadow under/beneath, with the translation of the last word differing slightly in the typescript (SD/247) and manuscript (VT24/12). In ordinary English the phrase might be the Children of Eru fell under shadow.

The subject Eruhinim of the sentence is the plural form of #. The verb dubdam seems to be in the form of # to fall, glossed in past tense because it is in a narrative occurring in the past. The verb has the plural marker in agreement with the number of the subject. The word under, beneath is suffixed to the noun it modifies, as is usual of Adunaic .

The previous (second draft) version of this sentence (SD/312) differs only in its use of the verb form dubbudam ( tense) instead of the final versions form dubdam (). The first draft version used all the same words but differed in its grammar.

The first draft of the 2nd phrase of the (SD/311). It differs from the final version only in grammar. The subject of the sentence seems to be a simple plural of #, not in the subjective case. The verb might be inflected with the 3rd-person singular masculine suffix u- he, but this contradicts the plurality of the subject. Another explanation is that the verb is in the tense and the initial u- is an augment vowel. Either way, it is difficult to explain why it has the verbal suffix -nim instead of the usual plural suffix .

The word under comes before the noun rather than as a suffix as is usual of later Adunaic . The word it modifies seems to be the case of the word shadow, indicating that the objects of prepositions could be declined into various cases in the draft grammar.
A feminine suffix appearing in several names, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/11). On SD/427, Tolkien said that the affix -th was often found in feminine forms.
One of the roots Tolkien used to illustrate various processes of Primitive Adunaic word formation (SD/422-5). It also seems to be the basis of words related to stars, such as .

A collective-noun meaning all the stars of the heavens, as opposed to which was used for an individual star (SD/427). The element gimil appears in many names, including several later names in The Lord of the Rings and The Silmarillion. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/15) that it may be related to the Elvish root shine (white).

Andreas Moehn suggested (/KH-B-L) that if the later name means Silver-fire, its initial element gimil could instead mean silver, perhaps as a cognate of Dwarvish . If so, this alternate meaning could either be a homonym of gimil stars, or a new meaning for gimil in Tolkiens later works.
A title of the goddess (Q. ) translated Star-kindler (SD/428), and therefore the Adunaic equivalent of S. . The first element means stars, and the second is an for the verb to kindle (SD/427-8).

Second son of the 18th ruler of Numenor Ar- (Q. Tar- *Light-sword) and younger brother to the 19th ruler Ar- (UT/227). The first element means stars. The second element most likely means sword if his fathers Quenya and Adunaic names have the same meaning.

Gimilzôr was the Adûnaic name of (SD/380) in the story “The Notion Club Papers” from the mid-1940s. Since the element means “stars”, this name is most likely a translation of the Sindarin name, which means “Star-foam”.

In later writings, Gimilzôr is the son of Ar- and the 23rd ruler of Númenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- (S/268). It is unclear whether this instance of Gimilzôr retains the same meaning as the earlier version of the name. It is possible that the later version has the same meaning as Telemnar (translated by most authors as “Silver-fire”), in which case Tolkien may also have revised the Adûnaic name of Elros (the word for “foam” was elsewhere given as Ad. roth). Alternately, it could be that the Adûnaic and Quenya names are unrelated, and Tar-Telemnar simply adopted the Adûnaic name of his illustrious ancestor.

Andreas Moehn suggested (/KH-B-L) that if Gimilzôr means “Silver-fire”, its initial element gimil “silver” could be a cognate of Dwarvish . Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/11) that his Quenya name Telemnar contains adjective ᴹQ. “of silver”, and does not involve “fire” at all.
conceptualDevelopment: As a name for Eärendil, this name first appeared as (SD/363).

descriptionText: Another name for Numenor translated Starwards (SD/378), the equivalent of Q. . Its first element is stars with the Adunaic and its second element is the suffix -ad () toward, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/15).
A noun translated star (SD/431) or star (in the sky) (SD/427), and fully declined on SD/431 as an example of a Strong II noun.

Christopher Tolkien mentions this as a noun meaning star from early and unpublished materials related to The Notion Club Papers stories (PM/372). It may be an element in the early Adunaic name for . As Indilzar was replaced by , it is likely that azar was replaced by and , which are well attested in later writings.
An example phrase indicating how Adunaic <a l="ad" v="numbers"/> follow plural nouns and are in a <a l="ad" v="genitive"/> relations with them: seven of stars (SD/427-8).
An example illustrating the difference between the singular noun star and the collective-noun (all) stars as used in the name Star-kindler, kindler of all the stars (SD/428).

A number translated as seven, appearing in the form hazad in the (SD/247), but in the form hazid in Lowdhams Report (SD/427-8). Helge Fauskanger suggested (/Adunaic) it may be related to the dwarvish word Khazad Dwarves, who were divided into seven houses.

This element appears to be the object pronoun me in the phrase dont touch me (SD/250). It is not clear whether it could also serve as a subject pronoun I. Thorsten Renk instead suggested (/18) that -he may be a marker for the , and proposed the invented word Ad. !ni for I, me, a hypothetical cognate of Q. .

A Primitive Adunaic form attested as i she (SD/435), but given the later feminine pronoun Ad. , the actual primitive pronoun must have been *HI [xi]. The suffix -i was also a common feature of Classical Adunaic .

A pronominal prefix, the feminine singular pronoun she (SD/247). It appears in the pseudo-phrase hi-Akallabeth She-that-hath-fallen in the sentence and in the verb form hikalba [she] fell in the sentence Numenor beloved fell (down). See the entry on for more discussion.

A patronymic suffix appearing in Eruhin Children of God (SD/247) and in the early phrase *Line of Elros [son] of Earendil (SD/382). It apparently means child. A possible feminine variant -hil appears in the early name Zimrahil (SD/373), later changed to .

Andreas Moehn suggested () that -hin might have been replaced by the suffix appearing in the later name ?Shore-son. However, the suffixes -hin and -thor (along with daughter) could have co-existed in the same way that Quenya suffixes Q. -son and Q. -daughter co-existed with the use of Q. child as a patronymic in names like Q. .

As suggested by several authors (/15, /KHIN), -hin is almost certainly related to Q. , S. child, either a direct loan or derived from the same root . Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/16) that the variant -hil in Zimrahil actually means heir, related to S. , Q. , and that this element also appears in Ad. .
A noun translated as ear and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/430).

A Primitive Adunaic form attested as u he (SD/435), but given the later Adunaic pronoun Ad. or hu he, the actual primitive pronoun may have been *U [u], *U or *HU [xu], as Tolkien indicated in a footnote (SD/433, note #7). The suffix -u was also a common feature of Classical Adunaic .
A suffix used to form feminine nouns from common or masculine nouns (SD/435). Another common variant was -e (SD/438).

The inflection used to mark nouns as plural (S/429), used either as a suffix (for weak-nouns) or replacing the last vowel (for strong-nouns). According to Tolkien, the primitive form of this suffix was most likely (SD/424). See the entry on the case for further details.

A word translated now in the (SD/247). In the final manuscript version, this is the only form of the word, but in the final typescript version and in all earlier versions, it sometimes appears in the form idon.

Some authors have suggested this variation occurs when ido appears before words beginning in a vowel or semi-vowel (/Adunaic, /12), but this seems unlikely to me. Carl Hostetter, Patrick Wynne and Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/18, /16, , /DAW) that idon is a inflection of the word ido, being used as a noun. The key evidence supporting this second theory is that where the form idon appears, its gloss is always now (is) rather than simply now. As discussed elsewhere (SD/429), the inflection can function as the verb to be.

I tend to agree with this theory of Hostetter, Wynne and Moehn, but I think the actually development is somewhat more complex. In the first draft version of the Lament of Akallabeth, this form of the word appears twice as idon lo! now is. As noted by Mr. Moehn (), this version of the Lament used a predicate suffix is in several places: burodan heavy-is, rokhi-nam bent-are. It seems likely that draft form idon lo! now is is another variation of this earlier syntax.

The draft predicate suffix differed from the later case in that it applied to the predicate of a clause instead of the subject. Compare these changes from the draft to final versions:

  • agannulo burudan death-shade heavy-is >> agannalo buroda death-shadow [is] heavy
  • batani rokhi-nam ways bent-are >> batina lokhi ways (are) bent

In both draft sentences, the subject is uninflected and the predicate has the predicate suffix -n/-nam. Conversely, in the later sentences the subject is inflected into the subjective case while the predicate is uninflected. This demonstrates the functional shift in the use of the predicate suffix -n in these drafts to the later use of the subjective inflection.

In both the second draft and final typescript versions of the Lament, the form idon was retained in all the sentences where it appeared in the first draft. This means that it could have been a remnant of this earlier syntax. The form idon could be reinterpreted as the sentences subject, but this is also problematic, since ido is certainly neuter and its subjective form should be *idowa, not idon.

It is my belief that Tolkien eventually decided that the suffix -n could no longer be used in this context and removed it, switching to an uninflected ido now everywhere in the text as is the case in the final manuscript version of the Lament. On the basis of this deduction, I also believe that the manuscript version was written after than the typescript version.

The 12th phrase of the (VT24/12). The first word is the adverb now and the second is the adjective all. Curiously, the adjective katha is not pluralized to agree with the noun as is the case with adjectives elsewhere in the text, including the pluralized lokhi at the end of this very sentence.

The subject batina roads is the plural form of the noun road, path, way. There is no verb, so the subjective form functions as the to be verb (SD/429). The final word lokhi seems to be a pluralized adjective, perhaps #.

The typescipt version has katha instead of katha, but is otherwise identical to the manuscript except some minor differences in translation (SD/247).

The first draft of the 12th phrase of the (SD/312). Although all of its word are similar to the final version, each has differences in grammar or spelling from the later versions of the text.

  • The first word ido is the same as in the final version, but is glossed lo! now instead of simply now.
  • The adjective kathi all is the plural form of , not singular as it is in the final text, perhaps indicating a shift in the rules for adjective-noun agreement.
  • The subject batani ways is the normal plural form of , not inflected to the case as it is in the final text.
  • The final word rokhi-nam (are) bent has the plural adjective rokhi instead of later form lokhi. It also use the suffix -nam are, likely the plural of the predicate suffix is. This probably serves the same function as the inflection of the final version: to represent the to be verb are.
This noun is another singular variation of the collective-noun (all) stars, used for a star-shaped figure (SD/427) instead of an actual star which is .
A suffix used in plural inflections of , in most cases blending with the plural ending -i to become -im (SD/430).
The suffix for singular , reduced to -n when the noun ends in a vowel (SD/430, 436).

A draft Adunaic phrase for the members of the elder house (SD/365, 382) which appears with and without the patronymic suffix . Though untranslated, Indilzar Azrabelo seems to mean Elros of Earendil, and the patronymic -hin probably means the line of ... or the house of ... or more literally *child, the last translation suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/13). This phrase uses an earlier form for the Adunaic name of (instead of later ) and an earlier form Azrabel of the Adunaic name of his father (instead of later ). It also seems to include the suffix , although this could also be the inflection.
A noun meaning flower or more specifically lily (PE19/99). It appears as an element in Adunaic names from the 1940s (Rothinzil, SD/360) and later (Inziladun, LotR/1035).

Son of Ar- and and the 24th ruler of Numenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- The Farsighted (LotR/1035). The meaning of his Adunaic name is Flower of the West (UT/227), so he is an example of a Numenorean ruler whose Adunaic and Quenya names had different meanings. The name Inziladun was his given name and he adopted Palantir when he ascended the throne.

As pointed out by Andreas Moehn (/JIL), the ordering of the elements in this name are inconsistent with the rules outlined in Lowdhams Report, which indicate that the adjectival element West should come before the noun Flower that it modifies (SD/428), so that the name properly should be *Aduninzil, similar to Lord of the West. The name as written would mean West of the Flower. Perhaps Tolkien relaxed or altered those rules in his later writings.

The wife of Ar- who was the 23rd ruler of Numenor (S/268). She was a secret Elf-friend and raised her son to be faithful to the Valar. Her name has the same initial element as her son: flower. The second element might be word.

A suffix used for the names of languages, appearing only in , the languages of the (SD/414). My best guess for the form of this suffix is *-iye with Nimir reduced to Nimr- by the Adunaic . If the first element is instead Nimri (perhaps an adjective meaning Elvish), the suffix could be *-ye or even *-e, with the y inserted as the usual after the final -i.

An adjective glossed “straight” (SD/247), “right” (VT24/12) and “true” (SD/427), the last of these in the compound “true-sayer”. This final example is interesting, because the adjective izindi is declined into the case.
conceptualDevelopment: In its first appearance (SD/312), the form of this adjective was ezendi, an impossible form in the later phonetic rules of Lowdham’s Report, since Adûnaic only allowed the long vowel (SD/423).

descriptionText: A noun for prophet, more literally true-sayer, given by Tolkien as an example of the case combined with a verb stem in an (SD/427).

The primitive form of sweetheart, beloved (SD/424), probably derived from the root Ad. . The actual primitive word was more likely *izrai, produced via from the biconsonantal form *izri. Its plural form izray+yi is also attested.
A noun translated sweetheart, beloved and fully declined as an example of a weak II feminine-noun (SD/438).
A (primitive?) masculine suffix used in the formation of (male) baby from the root Ad. MIYI (SD/427). Tolkien stated that that k was one of the favoured masculine consonants (SD/427).
A noun appearing only as an element in city folk (SD/435).
A compound noun translated city folk given as an example of an adjectival-genitive relationship between nouns (SD/435).

A word glossed and so in both the draft and final versions (SD/247, 311). This is the only known Adunaic conjunction. Andreas Moehn suggested (/DAW, KA3) that the element -do is some sort of modifying suffix, also seen in and , so that the conjugation and is simply ka. Thorsten Renk also used ka for simple and (/15).

The 1st phrase of the (SD/247). It changed little from its original draft, with only the verb unekku becoming unakkha. Tolkien did not interpret the name Zigurun in any version of the text, but it can be equated to Sauron from information given elsewhere (SD/250). Tolkiens gloss was and so humbled he-came, which in more ordinary English might be and so Sauron he came humbled.

The subject Zigurun of the sentence is the form of the name . The verb unakkha has the 3rd-person singular masculine inflection u- he. In the grammatical rules of Lowdhams Report, the subject would be emphasized with this syntax (SD/429), so the sense might be more like and it was Sauron who came humbled. It could be that the so of the English gloss is a representation of this emphasis, and that the initial word is simply the conjugation and.

The verb form nakkha is the tense of to come. Since the majority of the text seems to be in the , this use of the past tense would function as a pluperfect according to the grammatical rules of Lowdhams Report (SD/439). If so, the sense would be more like Sauron had come rather than Sauron came. Finally, the position of the adjective humbled is difficult to explain, since Tolkien stated that adjectives normally preceded nouns (SD/428). Perhaps it follows because it is used as a predicate of the subjective subject Zigurun (a construction discussed on SD/429), so that the literal interpretation of the full phrase would be *and so Sauron [was] humbled, he had come [to Numenor]. Alternately, zabathan could appear in this abnormal position because it is a (verbal adjective).

The first draft of the 1st phrase of the (SD/311), differing only from the the final version in its use of the verb (h)unekku for later unakkha. In the draft, Tolkien changed the 3rd-person singular masculine suffix in this sentence from hu- to u- as he vacillated over the proper form of this inflection.
A Primitive Adunaic root gloss fall (SD/416) appearing as an element in the name (PM/158) and also most likely the basis for the verb to fall (down).

A verb translated fall down (SD/439). This verb has more conjugations than any other attested Adunaic verb, and is therefore useful for studying the Adunaic verb system. Excluding the first draft of the , it appears in four forms: ukallaba [he] fell (SD/429), hikallaba she fell (down) (SD/427), hikalba she fell (VT24/12) and yakalubim lean over (SD/251). Andreas Moehn suggested (, /KALB) the last of these could be a different verb kalub- to lean, but I think it is likelier to be a form of kalab-, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/26-27).

Various verbal prefixes and suffixes can be extracted by comparison to other forms: the pronominal prefixes u- he, hi- she and ya- they (neuter), as well as the plural verb suffix . Removing these elements, we have three distinct forms: kallaba fell, kalba fell and kalubi lean over. These likely represent distinct verb tenses. The question is: which ones?

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/26-27) that kalubi is most likely the with the literal sense *are falling over, a conclusion with which most other authors agree (/Adunaic, /14). Andreas Moehn agreed on this verb tense (, /KALB), but suggested that it is from the verb kalub- to lean instead.

The two remaining forms kalba and kallaba both have the gloss fell. This ambiguity is because the Adunaic tense could used to describe the past in a narrative (SD/439). Most authors agree that these forms are the Adunaic and tenses respectively, though Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested that kallaba is the instead (/27-28). See the entry on the Adunaic tense for further discussion.

Finally, there is form appearing only in the draft versions of the Lament: akallabi fell in ruin. I believe this is an example of tense; see that entry for further discussion.
A noun translated woman (SD/434).
A verb translated hold, given by Tolkien as an example of a <a l="ad" v="biconsonantal-verb"/> (SD/439). There is unfortunately no information on how it might be conjugated.
An unglossed root (SD/415), likely the basis for the noun horse (SD/434).
A noun translated horse, given by Tolkien as an example of how can be altered into masculine and feminine forms using the suffixes and : karbi mare and karbu stallion (SD/434).

A word translated all in the (SD/288, VT24/12). This word appeared in the form katha in the final typescript version of the Lament (SD/247), but in all other instances appeared as katha. If the final typescript is later than the final manuscript, katha may be its final form, but I believe that the manuscript was later, and katha better matches its appearance as an element in conqueror (SD/429). This last example is interesting in that it is an example of an adjective declined into the case.

A noun translated conqueror (SD/429), apparently a compound whose first element seems to be the form of all. The final element is likely the agental suffix also attested in and . If so, the middle element is probably a verb, perhaps a triconsonantal verb *, though it could be a derived verb *phazga-.

A Primitive Adunaic word glossed crow (SD/426). Tolkien gave two primitive forms of this word, khaw and khaw, which could just be variant forms of the same root *KHAW. A more intriguing possibility is that khaw is actually the form of khaw, since this would indicate that this subjective formation dates back to the primitive stages of the language. As evidence of this, the derived plural khawi(m) (SD/426) does resemble the Classical Adunaic subjective plural.

Contradicting this conjecture is the fact that khaw, as an animal name, should be declined as a common-noun, using the common subjective suffix . Elsewhere, though, Tolkien declined some animal names as if they were neuter nouns, for example narika as the subjective plural of # (SD/251). Perhaps not all animals were common nouns, or perhaps Tolkiens ideas for the subjective tense were not fully formed when these examples were written.

A verb appearing only as akhaini lay in the first draft of the Lament of Akallabeth (SD/312). In later versions of the Lament it was change to the verb to go, but since this replacement has a different sense, perhaps khay- remains valid.

This verb is only attested in the form akhaina lay and like all the draft verbs is difficult to analyze. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne analyze its initial element as the 3rd-singular pronominal suffix a- and its final element -ni as a past tense marker (/34, 37), also suggesting it may be derived from the Elvish root lie (down) (/10). This Elvish derivation seems likely to me, but I think the form of the verb may instead be the .

Thorsten Renk suggested (/35) the verb stem may instead be khain-. While he could be right about its use in the draft Adunaic language, this doesnt fit the later phonetic rules of Lowdhams Report, which allow only long in Classical Adunaic (SD/423).
A noun translated spring and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/430).

A noun translated crow (SD/426). Tolkien listed this noun in two forms, khau and kho, both as examples of seemingly uniconsonantal nouns that prehistorically were biconsonantal (from prehistoric khaw). Most authors have suggested these are simply variations on the same noun illustrating different paths of phonetic development (/18, /Adunaic). Another interesting possibility is that khau is an (archaic?) form of kho, produced from the usual a-fortification of primitive khaw khaw, which would develop phonetically in Classical Adunaic to khau and kho. As support for this idea, the plural form of khau is given as khawi(m), which appears to include the subjective plural suffix .

This line of reasoning is quite speculative. Nevertheless, it is probably easier to use the form kho over khau, since the inflections of kho would be more regular: plural khoi, dual *khowat, objective *khowu, etc.

An element meaning lord appearing only in the name Lord of the West, though a similar form appears in the earlier names Lord and Lord of Darkness. It isnt clear whether this element is *akhor or *khor, but khor resembles the Primitive Elvish root rule, govern, possess, to which it may be related.

This possible relationship has been suggested by various authors (/Adunaic, /KHUR). Andreas Moehn rejected the relationship, pointing out that Primitive Elvish kheru lord would have developed phonetically into Ad. **khiru (). However, khor may be derived from some more ancient Avari loan word, which underwent different phonetic developments than those of the Eldarin languages, perhaps kher- > khar > khaur > Ad. khor.
A pronominal prefix, most likely the second person pronoun you, appearing in the verb kitabdahe [you] touch me in the sentence (SD/250). See the entry on for more discussion.

A noun appearing only in its plural form kulbi roots, corresponding to the collective-noun roots, edible vegetables that are roots not fruits (SD/431). As such, it most likely refers to root vegetables only, rather than other senses of the English word root.

One of the Primitive Adunaic roots Tolkien used to illustrate the processes of Primitive Adunaic word formation (SD/422-5). It also seems to be the root of words such as and root (as a kind of plant) (SD/431), perhaps an deliberate pun by Tolkien.

englishWord: roots, edible vegetables that are roots not fruits
descriptionText: A collective-noun meaning all edible root vegetables, as opposed to used for an individual root (SD/431).
