A noun appearing only as an element in city folk (SD/435). It may be related to Q. people, as suggested by various authors (/18, /Adunaic, /LAI). In at least one Avari dialect, this word was lai (WJ/410).
An adjective variously glossed as “bent” or “crooked”, attested only in its plural form lôkhî (SD/247, VT24/12). Andreas Moehn suggested (/LUKH) it may be related to the Elvish root √ “bend, loop”.
conceptualDevelopment: In its first appearance, this adjective had the plural form rōkhī, suggesting an earlier singular form *rôkho (SD/312).

descriptionText: A noun translated night or more fully fair night, a night of stars, a late loan word from Q. (SD/414-5). According to Tolkien, it has a pleasant connotation similar to its Quenya equivalent: it is a word of peace and beauty and has none of the associations of fear or groping that dark has (SD/306). Some unpleasant words for night and darkness are , and .
A suffix appearing in Adunaic verbs that have plural subjects. See <a l="ad" v="plural verbs"/> for further discussion.
A prepositional suffix translated “with” (SD/247, 429).
conceptualDevelopment: At an earlier conceptual stage, it was the grammatical inflection used for the (SD/438).

descriptionText: The suffix used for the case, translated with (SD/438). In a later conceptual stage, it became the ordinary prepositional suffix . Carl Hostetter and Partick Wynne suggested (/33, /19) that the deleted form -men on SD/311 is a separate prepositional suffix on related to MQ. place, but I believe it is a variant of the plural instrumental form -main.

A hypothetical verb from which the wright, *builder is derived, itself attested only as an element in the name Shipwright. It may be related to the Elvish root M use, handle, as suggested by Andreas Moehn (/MAG).
A noun meaning wright attested only as an element in the name Shipwright (PM/151). It seems to be an of a verb ? build with the agental suffix . Therefore, its literal sense might be *builder.
The primitive form of spirit (SD/424). Its plural form manaw+yi is also attested.

A noun translated spirit and fully declined as an example of a Weak II noun (SD/438). It appeared with both a short a (SD/424) and long a (SD/438). Given its ending -o, it might be a masculine-noun, but it seems unlikely that spirits would only be male. This entry assumes it is a common-noun instead. It is probably related to MQ. departed spirit as suggested by various authors (/19, /Adunaic, /MAN).
An unglossed word that it is apparently the masculine equivalent of baby girl, using the masculine suffix (SD/427).

An Adunaic noun for the heaven or sky, cognate of Q. but not a direct loan word from Quenya (SD/241). It was borrowed from Primitive Elvish, probably from an Avari dialect, and therefore underwent different phonetic development (SD/414). In one place Tolkien changed it minil (SD/414), but the form minal appears in various compounds and is probably to be preferred.
A draft Adunaic word for the heavens, later replaced by (SD/305).

A non- that contrasts with the name Pillar of Heaven (SD/429). Since the phrase is not objective, it must be a genitive relationship, who meaning according to Tolkien was something like a pillar in the sky, or made of cloud.

The name of a planet in Tolkiens unfinished story The Notion Club Papers, translated Poise in Heaven (SD/200). Its language is not specified, but it is probably Adunaic, since its first element is the Adunaic word for heaven. If so, its second element must mean poise.

A Primitive Adunaic root glossed heaven, sky that Tolkien used as an example of an early borrowing from Primitive Elvish: the Primitive Elvish root became Ad. MINIL from whatever Avari language influenced Primitive Adunaic (SD/414).

The Adûnaic name of the Pillar of Heaven (Q. ), the great and holy mountain at the center of Númenor (SD/249). The first element is the objective form of “the heavens”. The second element “pillar” is normally a noun, but in this case it behaves verbally with the sense “that which supports”, since the case requires a second verbal element (SD/429). Therefore, the literal translation of the name is “That Which Supports the Heavens”.
conceptualDevelopment: The first Adûnaic name for this mountain was Menel-tūbil or (SD/305, SD/363).

descriptionText: An Adunaic noun for little or baby girl (SD/427, 437), fully declined on SD/437 as an example of a Weak I noun. It is also given as an example of a feminized noun form on SD/427.

A root glossed small that Tolkien wrote in its Ad. MIYI (SD/427). For consistency this entry has normalized it to the basic form of biconsonantal roots. Although glossed as small, all of its attested derivatives have to do with babies.
A noun attested only in its dual form miyat (infant) twins (SD/427). Its masculine and feminine equivalents are and .

The Adûnaic name of ; it seems to be a loan word from Q. “Mighty Arising” (or some Avari variant of it), but it is glossed “Lord of Darkness” (SD/358). If this is the meaning of the word, the final element could be related to “lord” appearing in the later name “Lord of the West”, or to the older rejected name “Lord”, also referring to Melkor. The initial element Mul- could perhaps be a distant variation on the Elvish root √ “dark”. Yet another possibility is that it was originally an ancient Elvish loan word (✶milikûr?) that shifted in form to resemble the meaning “Lord of Darkness”.
conceptualDevelopment: The first Adûnaic name for Morgoth, Mēlekō, was more clearly based on ᴹQ. , which was the Quenya name for Melkor in that stage of Tolkien’s writing.

descriptionText:
A suffix appearing at the end of several words in the first draft of Lament of Akallabeth, variously glossed with different forms of the verb to be: burudan heavy-is, rokhi-nam bent-are, idon now is (SD/312). Evidentally the suffix -n is is the singular form and -nam are is plural. The plural form probably includes the plural verbal suffix . This use of the suffix -n is probably no longer be valid in later versions of Adunaic, as discussed below.

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/36) that -nam maybe related to Q. to be, but they fail to analyze the singular forms of the suffix. Andreas Moehn () does connect the singular instances of the suffix -n to the plural -nam, but without connecting it to Q. na-. I think both authors got part of the story right: the suffixal form -na is most likely derived from the same Elvish root as Q. na-, losing its final a in the singular form but preserving it in the plural form when the plural suffix -m is added.

In its first two appearances in the draft version of the Lament, this suffix is attached to the predicate of a copula (a linguistic term for a to be expression). For that reason, the discussion here uses the term predicate suffix for this use of the -n suffix:

  • agannulo burudan nenum death-shade heavy-is on-us
    subject agannulo death-shade, predicate buruda heavy + -n is.
  • ido kathi batani rokhi-nam lo! now all ways bent-are
    subject batani ways, predicate rokhi bent + -nam are.

The suffixs second two appearances in the draft version of the Lament are more ambiguous.

  • ephalek idon akallabeth far away lo!now is She-that-is-fallen.
  • ephal ephalek idon athanate far far away is now the Land of Gift.

Going by word order alone, it seems that the -n is attached to the predicate in both of these sentences as well. However, as Andreas Moehn points out (), ido could be the subject of both sentences if the predicates are the final word of each sentence, which is more consistent with the later subjective inflection.

In the later version of Adunaic described in Lowdhams Report, the suffix -n has a new function, namely as the common subjective suffix: -an/-n. This new use differs from the older one in that it applies to the subject of a copula instead of the predicate. Despite this grammatical change from draft-Adunaic, the word form idon appears in all later versions of the except the final manuscript version.

  • Ephalak idon Yozayan far away now (is) Land of Gift (SD/247).
  • Ephal ephalak idon hi-Akallabeth far far away now (is) She-that-hath-fallen (SD/247).

These later appearances of idon still have the gloss now (is), so it seems possible that these they are remnants of the predicate suffix from draft Adunaic. Moehn, Hostetter and Wynne all suggested (, /16) that these later appearances of idon can be reinterpreted as a inflection. However, this interpretation is still problematic, since ido would surely be a neuter instead of a common noun, whose subjective form would therefore be *idowa.

The suffix -n did not appear after ido in the final manuscript version of the Lament, and the gloss is was removed as well:

  • Ephalak ido Yozayan far away now Gift-land (VT24/12).
  • Ephal-ephalak ido hi Akallabeth far far away now She that hath Fallen (VT24/12).

It is my belief that Tolkien eventually decided that the suffix -n could no longer be used in this context and removed it.

A prepositional element only attested in the late (1968) word hind-track, referring to the wake behind a boat, so perhaps meaning *behind (PM/376). It appears only as a prefix, but in the earlier Adunaic grammar of Lowdhams Report (1946), Adunaic are used as suffixes (SD/435).

An Adunaic noun translated hind-track, referring to the wake behind a boat (PM/376). It appeared more than two decades (1968) after Tolkiens Adunaic Grammar in Lowdhams Report from the 1940s (SD/413-440). This noun is inconsistent with the earlier grammar in two respects. First, the prepositional element nad- appears as a prefix, not as a suffix as did in the earlier grammar (SD/435). Second, it includes a short o, whereas in the earlier phonetic rules of Adunaic, only a long is allowed (SD/423). See the entry on for further discussion.

An otherwise unexplained root that Tolkien used to illustrate the processes of Primitive Adunaic word formation (SD/422-3). It may have no real meaning. Even if it were, certainly only a few of its derivatives could be real words in Classical Adunaic.
A Primitive Adunaic root glossed come, approach (SD/416), no doubt the basis for the verb to come.

A verb translated in the past tense as “came” (SD/247, 311), so probably meaning “to come”. Like , this is one of the few Adûnaic verbs attested in more than one conjugation. As such, it is useful in the study of Adûnaic verbs, in this case s as opposed to triconsonantal kalab-.

It is attested in two forms, unakkha “he-came” and yanākhim “are at hand”. The initial elements in these forms are the 3rd-sg masculine pronominal prefix u- and the 3rd-pl neuter pronominal prefix ya-, respectively, while the latter form has the plural verbal suffix . Removing these elements leaves the conjugated forms nakkha and nākhi, which are the and tenses according to the theories used here. If the second form is the continuative-present, its literal meaning may be “are coming”.
conceptualDevelopment: In the draft version of the Lament of Akallabêth, this verb stem was apparently nek-, with past forms hunekkū >> unekkū “he-came”, with Tolkien vacillating on the proper form of the 3rd-sg masculine pronominal prefix u-.

descriptionText: A noun attested only in the compound agannâlô “death-shadow [is]” (SD/247, VT24/12). The first element of the compound, “death”, as identified elsewhere (SD/426), so the remaining element must mean “shadow”. The compound is the subject of the sentence “death-shadow [is] heavy on us” and is therefore in the case. According the grammatical rules of Lowdham’s Report, the only possibly normal form producing this subjective is nâlu: compare “moon” to its subjective form nîlô (SD/431).
conceptualDevelopment: In early writings, the compound was (non-subjective) agannūlo, so that the apparent draft form of this noun was nūlo. A similar form nūlu appears on SD/306, described only as “a word with the evil sense of ‘night’ or ‘dark’”. It could be a separate word or another variation of this word, with the development nūlo >> nūlu >> nālu. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/21) that the earlier forms may be related to ᴹQ. “dark, dusky, obscure”.

descriptionText: A noun attested only in the plural form Narika eagles (SD/251). This formation is peculiar, because it seems to be a neuter subjective form, but the names of animals are generally , as pointed out by Andreas Moehn (/NARK). If it were declined as a common noun, the subjective plural should be *narkim: compare Elf whose subjective plural form is nimrim (SD/436). Perhaps when Narika was written, Tolkien had not finished working out the Adunaic gender and case system.
A noun translated soldier and fully declined as an example of a masculine Weak II noun (SD/438). Several authors have suggested (/20, /NERE) that it may be related to man.

englishWord: The Eagles of the Lords of the West are at hand
descriptionText:
An isolated Adunaic sentence in The Notion Club Papers story (SD/251). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/26) that this same sentence is mentioned previously on SD/231 where Lowdham speaks in an unknown tongue, and then cries out in English Behold the Eagles of the Lords of the West! They are coming over Numenor!. If so, this provides another translation of the phrase.

The first word, Narika Eagles seems to be the plural of # eagle, but is unusual in that it is declined as if it were a neuter noun. The names of animals are generally (SD/426). Perhaps when this sentence was written, Tolkien had not yet fleshed out the Adunaic rules.

Narika is modified by the noun phrase nBari of the Lords, which is a combination of the genitive prefix of (elided) and the plural of the noun lord. This is also unusual in that it uses the short i rather than the long i for the plural, another sign that this may be an early sentence (the Adunaic often used a short i).

The phrase is further modified by nAdun of the West, another instance of an elided genitive prefixed to the noun west.

The verb yanakhim is glossed are at hand. Its initial element ya- is likely the third neuter person plural pronominal suffix they and it ends with the normal plural verb suffix . This leaves the verb form nakhi, which seems to be an inflection of the verb come. A literal interpretation might be *The Eagles of the Lords of the West are coming, as supported by the second translation mentioned above, so that this is an example of the Adunaic tense. This analysis of yanakhim was suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/27).

A noun translated soldier and fully declined as an example of an (archaic) masculine Strong II noun (SD/437). The archaic form of this word is naru which is a Strong II noun since it ends in a single short vowel. Its non-archaic form is naru, which is presumably declined as a Weak II noun; most masculine and feminine nouns became weak in Classical Adunaic (SD/436). It may be related to the Primitive Elvish root , as suggested by several authors (/20, /Adunaic, /NERE).

A first person plural object pronoun us attested only in the prepositional phrase on us in the , developing though the various drafts as nenum >> nenu >> nenud (SD/247, 312). Most authors identify the element ne as the pronoun (/20, , /14), which seems likely since the prepositional element is probably -num/nu/nud related to Q. under. It is not clear whether this pronoun can also be used as a subject pronoun we, or if it must always be an object us.
The masculine personification of the moon (SD/426), perhaps the Adunaic name for Q. .

A noun translated as moon and fully declined as an example of a Strong II noun (SD/431). It appears with both a short and long final -u, but Tolkien indicated that the form with long u is actually the personified form Man in the Moon (SD/426), perhaps the Adunaic name of . Tolkien also listed the later forms Nil, Njul (SD/306), one of which may be the Westron word for moon, most likely Wes. . Andreas Moehn suggested (/NUL) that this noun may be related to nulo/nulu/nalu, but given the evil connotations of these words (SD/306) and the different stem vowels, this seems unlikely to me.
A Primitive Adunaic root glossed shine (SD/416), apparently the basis for Elf.

A noun translated “Elf” (WJ/419) and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/436). In one place, its plural Nimrî was translated “Shining Ones” (SD/358), which indicates was probably derived from the Primitive Adûnaic root √.
conceptualDevelopment: In its earliest appearances from the 1940s, this noun had the plural form Nimrî (SD/358, 388) as opposed to later plural Nimîr (SD/388, 436), which could indicate either an earlier singular form Nimri or a variant syntax for formation. The word also appears in Tolkien’s Quendi and Eldar essay from 1959-60 (WJ/386), indicating that this word survived in Tolkien’s later conception of Adûnaic.

descriptionText: The Adunaic word for the Elvish language (SD/414), most likely a combination of the word Elf (evidently with the Adunaic ) and a suffix meaning language, perhaps .
The Adûnaic name for Q. “Elf-friend”, almost certainly with the same meaning (SD/247). The first element is the form of “Elf” and the second element is an for “*to love” (SD/389).
conceptualDevelopment: The first Adûnaic version of this name, Nimruzân, shares the same suffix as the first Adûnaic version of his father’s Adûnaic name .

descriptionText: A noun meaning “Elf-friend”, attested only in the () plural form Nimruzîrim (PM/151). It is identical to the Adûnaic name of Q. , which had the same meaning.
conceptualDevelopment: An earlier name for the faithful Númenóreans was (SD/347).

descriptionText: An early name of the Numenoreans who remained faithful to the Valar, later called the Elf-friends: Ad. Nimruzirim, Q. . It is not clear what language this word belongs to, but it may contain the word Adunaic word for the Valar: .

A noun translated girl and fully declined as an example of a feminine Strong I noun (SD/430). It is also used as an example of feminine nouns that use the suffix -i in their inflection as opposed to the usual -u: nithli (SD/431). Though not explicitly stated, nithli is also an example of the variant objective-with-syncope syntax discussed on SD/435. Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/21) it may be related to the Elvish root young.

A verb attested only as an in the names Star-kindler and kindler of a (particular) star (SD/428). Thorsten Renk suggested (/32) the base verb is nitir-, and this seems to me to be the likeliest possibility. Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/NITY) that the verb stem may be nit-, and that the -ir is some kind of feminine agental suffix.

A preposition attested only in the phrase on us in the , changing through the drafts as nenum >> nenu >> nenud (SD/247, 312). Most authors identify -nud as the prepositional element (/20, , /14), perhaps related to Q. under. If so, it may be a derivative of the Elvish roots under or down, with a semantic shift to the meaning on.

A noun translated fool and fully declined as an example of a Weak I noun (SD/437-8). It was later written in the form niph (SD/426), but since all the attested declensions are based on nuph, the entry here uses the earlier form.

The word nuph is a common-noun but it has some example inflections with masculine and feminine suffixes: nuphun (masculine subjective), nuphin (feminine subjective), nuphi (feminine objective). This seems to be another way that an individuals gender be indicated (male fool, female fool) instead of using explicit masucline and feminine suffixes like or .

A noun translated parent (SD/434). It also appears in the dual form nuphrat father and mother, but this dual form is peculiar. As a weak II noun, the dual form ought to be *nupharat, as for example road batanat pair of roads (SD/431). Its dual form seems instead to undergo the Adunaic (vowel loss), which happens nowhere else with a long vowel. There is no obvious explanation for this irregular formation.

A prepositional suffix translated “from” (SD/429). In a few places, the suffix appears with the v (pronounced ) between it and a preceding u-vowel (SD/247, 249). It is likely related to the Quenya genitive inflection Q. .
conceptualDevelopment: At an earlier conceptual stage, this suffix was a grammatical inflection, the (SD/438).

descriptionText: The suffix used for the case, with a plural form -om (SD/438). In a later conceptual stage, it became the ordinary prepositional suffix .

A prepositional element only attested in the late (1968) word fore-cutting (PM/376), referring to the wake before a boat, so perhaps meaning *before. It appears only as a suffix, but in the earlier Adunaic grammar of Lowdhams Report from the 1940s, Adunaic are used as suffixes (SD/435). This preposition also differs from the earlier phonetic rules of Lowdhams Report, which allow only long in Adunaic words. If this preposition were used in the grammatical and phonetic context of Lowdhams Report (Middle Adunaic), it might be the suffix *-ob. See the entry on for further discussion.

An Adunaic word translated fore-cutting, referring to the wake before a boat (PM/376). It appeared more than two decades (1968) after Tolkiens Adunaic Grammar in Lowdhams Report from the 1940s (SD/413-440). It is inconsistent with the earlier grammar in two respects. First, the prepositional element ob- appears as a prefix, not as a suffix as did in the earlier grammar (SD/435). Second, it includes a short o, whereas in the earlier phonetic rules of Adunaic, only a long is allowed (SD/423). See the entry on for further discussion.

A suffix appearing only in the name Golden and possibly also in . Since the element is elsewhere defined as gold (LotR/1114, SD/426), perhaps this suffix can be used to form from nouns in Adunaic. Andreas Moehn suggested (/ZIMR) it may instead be an agental suffix, a variant of .
A noun translated hand, given as an example of an apparent Adunaic uniconsonantal noun, which had a but lost one of its consonants from its ancient form Ad. (SD/416, 426).
A Primitive Adunaic root glossed hand, the basis for the noun of the same meaning (SD/416).
The Primitive Adunaic form of the noun hand (SD/426).
A noun meaning “gold”, the only Adûnaic word defined in The Lord of the Rings (LotR/1114).
conceptualDevelopment: This noun also appears in “Lowdham’s Report on the Adunaic Language” from the 1940s (SD/426).

descriptionText:
The son of who usurped the throne to become the 25th and final ruler of Númenor, translated “Golden” (LotR/1114, S/270). His Quenya name was Tar-. Since Calion appears to mean “*Son of Light”, Ar-Pharazôn is an example of a Númenórean ruler whose Adûnaic and Quenya names had different meanings.

The first element in his name is the noun “gold”. Since Pharazôn is glossed “Golden”, the second element may be an adjectival suffix. Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/PHAR’Z) that the name means “*Golden One”, closer to its Quenya equivalent, and that the suffix -ôn is a masculine variant of the agental suffix . Either way, the name is also notable in that it does not undergo the Adûnaic when its suffix is added.
conceptualDevelopment: The name also appeared in “The Notion Club Papers” from the 1940s (SD/311), in some examples inflected into the case (SD/247, 428-9).

descriptionText: A hypothetical verbal element in the noun conqueror (SD/429), whose literally meaning might be *all-ruler (kathu-phazg-an). Andreas Moehn suggested (/PHAZ) that it may be related to prince and have the meaning to rule, whereas Thorsten Renk suggested (/27) that it might mean to conquer.

A noun translated as prince, kings son, given as an example of a noun with a long vowel in its final syllable that (archaically) uses the declension for a , the rare class of Strong-Ib nouns (SD/436-7). By the time of Classical Adunaic, it could be declined as an ordinary instead.

An element appearing only in the name (UT/224). Though unglossed, her Quenya name seems to be jewel + daughter. The Adunaic element appears elsewhere as the Adunaic equivalent of Q. : in whose Quenya name is . These leaves the -phel to be daughter as suggested by several authors (/Adunaic, /PHIL), perhaps the feminine equivalent of son appearing in *Shore-son.

Phonetically, this element does not fit the earlier Adunaic phonetic rules of Lowdhams Report, which state that only a long was allowed in Adunaic (SD/423). When Tolkien wrote Lowdhams Report, Zimraphels Adunaic name was instead Zimrahil, so perhaps -hil was an earlier form of this suffix. If the suffix -phel were to be used in the phonetic context of the Adunaic of Lowdhams Report (Middle Adunaic) it might have the form *-phel. See the entry on for further discussion.

A verb translated to-gush or flow appearing in the (SD/247 SD/311), in later writings attested only in the form phursa. This form superficially seems to be the of the triconsonantal verb phurus-. Its two draft forms phurusam > phurrusim further support the idea that the verb stem is phurus-. However, ordinarily aorist forms end in a short -a, so perhaps there is something unusual about this formation. It also lacks the usual plural verb suffix appearing in first-draft version of the Lament, which would ordinally be required to agree with the plural subject. Since phursa appears with the or prefix du-, perhaps it is a special (infinitive?) form of the verb.

Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/PHUR) the verb stem may be phursa- instead of phurus, so that it is a . This isnt consistent with earlier forms, but it is possible that Tolkien changed his mind about the basic verb form.
A noun translated breath and fully declined as an example of a Weak I noun (SD/431).
A possible element in the verb to wage war, perhaps a causative suffix, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/24).

A noun translated dog and fully declined as an example of a Strong II noun (SD/437). It is also used as an example of a common-noun that can be altered to masculine and feminine forms rabo male dog and rabe bitch (SD/434).

A verb appearing in the with the past-tense translations “broke” and “rent” (SD/247, VT24/12), so meaning “to break, rend”. In the final version of the Lament it appeared as yurahtam “they rent”. The initial element of this form is the 3rd persons masculine plural suffix yu- “they”, while its final element is the plural verbal suffix , both in agreement with the plural subject Bârîm “Lords”. This leaves the basic verb form rahta, which is the tense according to the theories used here.

In the previous (second draft) version of the Lament, the verb form was urahta with the 3rd persons masculine singular suffix u- “he”, and no plural suffix -m. This is consistent with the subject in this version, which was the singular Bârun “Lord”.

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/22) that this verb may be related to Q. “to break” (MC/223). It could also be related to the contemporaneous ᴹQ. “to break asunder” (Ety/SKAT).
conceptualDevelopment: In the first draft of the Lament, the form was rakkhatū, indicating the earliest form of the verb may have had the verb stem rakhat- instead of later rahat-.

descriptionText: An element appearing in the name Foam-flower, attested in later writings (1968) as roth (PM/369, 376). This later form is incompatible with the earlier phonetic rules of Lowdhams Report from the 1940s, which allowed only long in Adunaic words. If this word were used in the phonetic context of Lowdhams Report (Middle Adunaic), it should be roth, and in these earlier texts, the Adunaic name of Earendis ship was Rothinzil with a long o (SD/360). Even in later writings, Tolkien lists ro ([ro] = roth) as one of its possible forms (PM/369). See the entry on for further discussion.

The Adunaic name of Earendils ship Foam-flower, of the same meaning (S/249). This name appears in earlier writings as Rothinzil with a long o (SD/360). Its later form is a violation of the phonetic rules laid out by Tolkien in Lowdhams Report, which said that the vowels and could only be long in Adunaic (SD/423). The later form could be an Anglicanized or a Westronized form (where a short could appear), or it could indicate that Tolkien changed his mind about Adunaic phonetic rules. Some linguistic notes from the 1930s suggest Tolkien at one point considered making the name Quenya (P19/49).
A word glossed shout (SD/426). Andreas Moehn suggested (/RUKH) that it may be a verb rukh- to shout, but it appears in a list of nouns, so I think it likelier that it is noun form.

This root, glossed scar, score, furrow, appeared as part of a discussion of the origin of the Sindarin word S. foam appearing in the name Star-foam (PM/368-371). Tolkien was uncertain whether this Sindarin word could coexist with its homophone S. copper-coloured, and investigated the possibility that Elros was instead derived from a Beorian word foam. According to Christopher Tolkien, his father was forced to abandon this line of reasoning when he remembered that the unrelated name S. also contained this element, forcing it to be of Sindarin rather than Beorian origin (SD/371).

Despite all this, the related Adunaic word Ad. roth foam survived in The Silmarillion in the Adunaic name Foam-flower of Earendils ship. Therefore, perhaps this root remains valid. According to Tolkien, this root originally had to do with ploughs and ploughing, and was later used for the white crest of waves by analogy with the churning dirt of a furrow (PM/376).
A noun translated “assent” (SD/247). The second element of this word is probably “word” as suggested by several authors (/22, /BITH). It isn’t clear what the first element means.
conceptualDevelopment: In the draft versions of the Lament of Akallabêth, the form of this word was sōbēth (SD/311).

descriptionText: This word is attested only in , whose Quenya name is (UT/223). The first element of the Quenya name seems to be shore, so the first element of his Adunaic name probably has the same meaning, as suggested by several authors (/22, /Adunaic, /SAKL).

The son of Ar- and the 22nd ruler of Numenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- (UT/223). Tolkien didnt translate either name, but his Quenya name seems to mean something like *Shore-son ( shore + -son) and his Adunaic name may have a similar meaning, as suggested by several authors (/22, /Adunaic, /SAKL). If so, the initial element * would mean shore and the suffix would mean -son.

The interpretation of the second element is less certain than the first. For example, Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/11) that is Quenya name Falassion is actually a genitive plural meaning of the Coasts and does not involve -son at all. They suggested the final -thor may instead mean one or lord (/23).
An otherwise unexplained root Tolkien gave to illustrate a pronunciation example. It may not be a real root.
A word Tolkien used to illustrate Adunaic pronunciation without giving its meaning (SD/421).
A Primitive Adunaic root glossed understand (SD/416), the basis for the verb to understand and the noun wise man (SD/421).

A verb attested only in the form usaphda he understood, an inflection with the 3rd person masculine pronominal prefix u- (SD/421). Archaically its aorist form underwent phonetic changes to become saptha, but it was later reformed to be consistent with other inflections of the verb (such as the tense *sapphada).
The primitive form of wise man, wizard, derived from the root Ad. (SD/421). Its final element may be a primitive form of the agental suffix .

A noun translated wise man, wizard given as an example of the phonetic development of primitive aspirates in contact with stops (SD/421). According to Tolkien, it was pronounced [safan], indicating that the combination pth would be pronounced as a voiceless labial fricative [f] followed by a voiceless dental fricative []. Given the phonetic rules of Adunaic, most voiceless stops would be pronounced as fricatives before another fricative in Classical Adunaic.

The Adunaic number two (SD/428). It seems likely that it is related to Q. two, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/22), though it is unclear how the initial s- might have developed in the Adunaic. It may also be related to the Adunaic dual suffix , as suggested by Andreas Moehn (/SAT).

A noun translated trump illustrating the development of Primitive Adunaic palatals, or <a l="pad" v="c-series"/> (SD/419). Perhaps its meaning is the older sense of the English word: trumpet; it seems unlikely it would refer to a suit of cards .

A noun translated mast illustrating the development of Primitive Adunaic palatals, or (SD/419). This example may also be related to the draft (?Adunaic) name for the Pillar of Heaven Meneltyula, which contains a word much like the cognate of sulum: Q. .

A verb translated touch, attested only in the phrase ba kitabdahe Dont touch me! (SD/250). The initial element is perhaps the 2nd person pronoun you, and the final element is perhaps the object pronoun me. This leaves the middle element tabda touch, which looks like the tense of a triconsonantal verb tabad-. Most authors agree with this decomposition of the verb (/TABD, /18, /Adunaic), though Thorsten Renk suggested (/18) the final element is a marker of the imperative.

An adverb glossed as both “once” and “then” (SD/247, VT24/12). Several authors have suggested (/23, /TA3) that the final element may be “now”. Andreas Moehn suggested (/TA3) the initial element tâ is a marker that puts it into the past: îdô = “now”, tâ-îdô = “previous time” = “then”. It seems likelier to me that the prefix is related to the Eldarin demonstrative root √ “that, there, then”, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/23): tâ-îdô = “that time” = “then”.
conceptualDevelopment: In the second draft of the , this word was ēluk (SD/312).

descriptionText: A noun translated smith and fully declined as an example of a masculine Strong I noun (SD/436). It may be related to the Eldarin root construct, as suggested by several authors (/23, /TAM).

The Adûnaic word for “pillar” (SD/241). Tolkien explained that this word is perceived as having a verbal function: “that which supports” (SD/429). As such, it can be used with an objective form in the name “That Which Supports the Heavens”.
conceptualDevelopment: In earlier drafts of “The Notion Club Papers” stories, this word appeared (SD/363), tūbil (SD/305) and (Quenya?) tyūlā (SD/346).

descriptionText: A draft version of pillar (SD/363), also appearing as tubil (SD/305) and tyula (SD/346), the latter perhaps a variant of Q. mast.
A (primitive?) feminine suffix used in the formation of baby girl from the root Ad. MIYI (SD/427). Tolkien stated that that th was one of the favoured feminine consonants (SD/427).
A noun translated land (SD/435) appearing in the Adunaic names for the Blessed Realm: and . Its Primitive Adunaic form was also , though its primitive was glossed realm" (SD/420).

The primitive form of land, written in allcaps as THANI (SD/420). Usually Tolkien used capitalization for primitive roots, but in this case it is more like to be a form derived from an unattested Primitive Adunaic root *THAN.

A phrase demonstrating the use of the genitive prefix , elided to n in this case (SD/435). Earlier in the same discussion, Tolkien gave the non-elided (but less common) variant: thani anAman. It may be contrasted with the genitive compound in which the adjective element appears first.

An element appearing only in the name (UT/223). Though unglossed, his Quenya name seems to be shore + son, so perhaps -thor is a patronymic meaning son, the masculine equivalent of daughter appearing in *Jewel-daughter, as suggested by Andreas Moehn (/THUR).

The inflection used to mark nouns in the case (SD/430), used either as a suffix (for weak-nouns) or replacing the last vowel (for strong-nouns). Feminine nouns sometimes use -i- instead for their objective forms (SD/432), owing to the association of the final vowel -u with masculinity.
A suffix used to form masculine nouns from common or neuter nouns (SD/435). Another common variant was -o (SD/438).

A well-attested pronominal prefix, the masculine singular pronoun he (SD/433). See the entry on for more discussion. Tolkien said that it had another variant hu- (SD/433), but this variant was only appears in the early and rejected hunekku, which was changed to unekku (see ). Tolkien further indicated that the form u- primitively had an initial consonant [] or [] that was lost (SD/433).

A noun translated shadow (SD/247), also described as a word with the evil sense of night or dark (SD/306). It appears in the preprositional phrase ugru-dalad under shadow (SD/247) and in the form ugrus horrorshadow (SD/311).
A verb translated overshadow, given as an example of a (SD/439). It appears to contain the element shadow, so perhaps the final element is a causative verbal suffix.
The suffix for singular (SD/430, 436), reduced to -n when the noun ends in a vowel.
The feminine personification of the sun (SD/426), perhaps the Adunaic name for Q. .

A noun translated sun (SD/306, 428). This word appears in the forms ure, uri and uri, but Tolkien declared that the form with long i is actually the personified form Lady of the Sun (SD/426), perhaps the Adunaic name of Q. . The form ure only appears once (SD/426), so uri is probably to be preferred as the ordinary word for Sun, especially since it is a neuter noun, which ordinarily cannot end in a long -e (SD/427). Tolkien lists the later forms Uir, Yr (SD/306), one of which may be the Westron word for sun, most likely Wes. . As suggested by several authors (/24, /UR), uri is probably derived from the Elvish root M.

An isolated Adunaic sentence in The Notion Club Papers story (SD/251). The subject urid seems to be the normal plural of mountain. According to the grammatical rules of Lowdhams Report, this word is not required to be in the subjective because the verb has the pronominal prefix ya-, most likely the neuter form of they. The verb ends with the usual verbal plural suffix , leaving the verb form kalubi. It seems to be an inflection of the verb to fall, perhaps the form. If so, a more literal translation of the sentence would be *the mountains are falling.

This analysis of yakalubim was suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/27).
A phrase demonstrating a dual compound with two different elements. It contains the related pair sun and moon (SD/428).
An example of a dual phrase with two different words. The first word of the pair is declined as a dual. It contains the related pair sun and moon (SD/428).

A noun attested only in its plural form urid mountains (SD/251). Several authors have suggested it is related to S. mountain, either borrowed directly or derived from the same Elvish root M (/24, /OROT).
A noun translated bear (SD/426), also given by Tolkien as an example of how can be altered into masculine and feminine forms using the suffixes and : urgi female bear, she-bear (SD/435).

A noun translated goblin, orc and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/436). Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/24) this form of the word may be a derivative of the contemporaneous Elvish root M. In later writings it appeared as Ad. urku/urkhu (WJ/390), a derivative of the Elvish root terrible shapes. This entry retains the form uruk because of its many attested inflections.

A pronominal prefix, most likely the neuter/common plural pronoun they. It appears in the verb yanakhim [they] are at hand in the sentence and in the verb yakalubim [they] lean over in the sentence (SD/251), both sentences having plural subjects. See the entry on for more discussion.

A verb appearing in the in the form ayadda “(it) went” (SD/247, VT24/12). Its initial element is the 3rd persons neuter plural suffix a- “it”. This leaves the basic verb form yadda, which is the tense according to the theories used here.
conceptualDevelopment: It appeared in the form yadda in the first draft version of the Lament, and this form was also briefly considered as a replacement for unakkha “he-came” in the first sentence of the Lament (SD/312).

descriptionText: The likely primitive form of the Classical Adunaic plural inflection (SD/429), appearing in a few examples of primitive plurals in the form -yi: manaw+yi, izray+yi (SD/424). Tolkien gave no indication of whether the primitive inflection was also used as an infix, as was the case for Classical Adunaic plurals of strong-nouns.
A hypothetical feminine plural pronoun they, assuming it follows the same pattern as masculine and neuter , as suggested by several authors (/Adunaic, /14, ).

An element in the name Land of Gift (UT/184, SD/241). The final element of this name is land, so its initial element yo most likely means gift, as suggested by several authors (/24, /Adunaic, /YAW), though Andreas Moehn points out this word could have the form yoz instead (/YAW).
This is the Adûnaic equivalent of Q. “Land of Gift”, one of the names given to the land of Númenor (UT/184, SD/241). Its final element is “land”, so its initial element * most likely means “gift”.
conceptualDevelopment: Tolkien experimented with many variations on this name before settling on Yôzâyan. The development seems to have been >> >> >> >> Yôzâyan, all of which were glossed “Land of Gift”.

descriptionText: A draft Adunaic name for the Land of Gift, later replaced by (SD/388). Its final element is land. Its initial element seems to be , which also appeared in its predecessor . If so, then abar probably meant gift at this stage, though its later meaning was strength, endurance, fidelity.

A draft Adunaic name for the Land of Gift, later replaced by (SD/378). Its initial element is a draft name for land also seen in the draft name for the Blessed Realm. Its final element seems to be , joined to the first element with an elided form of the genitive prefix of. If so, then at the time abar may have meant gift, but its later meaning was strength, endurance, fidelity.
A draft Adunaic name for the Land of Gift, later replaced by (SD/378). A variant of this name reappeared later as , the Adunaic name for the Blessed Realm.
The first-draft Adunaic name for the Land of Gift, later replaced by (SD/312).
A pronominal prefix, most likely the masculine plural pronoun they, appearing in the verb yurahtam [they] broke in the sentence (SD/247). See the entry on for more discussion.

A hypothetical verbal element in the participle adjective humbled (SD/247). According to Andreas Moehn (/ZABTH), Ales Bican suggested that the initial element za- is some kind of verbal prefix, similar in function to nu- in MQ. humbled, which would help explain why it does not undergo the Adunaic in its form.
An adjective translated humbled (SD/247, 311), perhaps a participle of the verb * to (be) humble with the participle suffix .
A noun translated house and fully declined as an example of a Strong I noun (SD/430).

An element appearing in the names (UT/227) and (UT/222). The Quenya name of Gimilzagar is , the final element of which means sword, so perhaps this word means the same thing. Most authors have suggested this interpretation (/24, /Adunaic, /ZAGR, /20) as well as its possible relationship to wage war.

A noun with alternate forms zaira and zair, glossed yearning and derived from the Primitive Adunaic root (SD/423). It also appears in the subjective form zaira longing (is) in the (SD/247), as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/25).

This words seems to be a violation of the rules for , under which a root never undergoes two changes from the same kind of process (SD/424). This word seems to have both kinds of vowel modification, and , from its root .

The 10th phrase of the (SD/247). The first word zaira longing (is) is the form of longing, yearning as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne (/20). Like in the 9th sentence, the phrase nenud is a combination of the pronoun us and the prepositional suffix on. There is no verb, so the subjective here functions as the verb to be (SD/429): longing (is) on us.

This sentence did not appear at all in the first draft of the Lament.
An Adûnaic word for “land” (SD/423). It has an irregular plural form zâin which is the result of the phonetic change (SD/423): . Thus, the archaic plural changed from †zâyîn > zâîn > zâin.
conceptualDevelopment: In earlier names this word appeared as (SD/378, 385).

descriptionText: An earlier version of land attested in a few early compounds (SD/378, 385), as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/25).

A prepositional suffix translated at (SD/429), but not appearing in any example sentences. It is perhaps a later repurposing of the case suffix , since the other became prepositional suffixes in later versions of the Adunaic grammar: draft genitive versus later preposition from, draft instrumental versus later preposition with.
The suffix used for the case (SD/438). It is attested in the in a plural form: avaloi-si Powers on (SD/311). In a later conceptual stage, it may have become the ordinary prepositional suffix at.
A word attested only in the compound Poise in Heaven (SD/200). Andreas Moehn suggested (/ZID) it may be related to straight.
The Adunaic name (or title) for (SD/250). It simply the word wizard used as a name.

A noun translated wizard and given as an example of a noun with a long vowel in its final syllable that (archaically) uses the declension for a (SD/437), the rare class of Strong-Ib nouns. By the time of Classical Adunaic, it could be declined as an ordinary instead. As the proper name , it was the Adunaic name for .

An element appearing in the names (UT/224) and (UT/222) and also the Hadorian name (WJ/234). The corresponding Quenya names Q. and Q. both seem to contain jewel, so this is the likely meaning of the Adunaic word as well, as suggested by most authors (/25, /Adunaic, /ZIMR).

The daughter of Ar- (Tar-), who would have been the 25th ruler of Númenor had the throne not been usurped by her cousin Ar- (UT/224). Her Quenya name Tar- seems to mean “*Jewel’s Daughter”. If her Adûnaic name has the same meaning, then the first element probably means jewel and the second element might mean “-daughter”, though it could simply be a general feminine suffix.
conceptualDevelopment: In her earliest appearance in the Tolkien’s stories, this character was called ᴹQ. (Tar-) (LR/27, SD/335, SD/351). Tolkien gave her the name Ad. Ar-Zimrahil after he invented the Adûnaic language (SD/373). The suffix -hil in this version of the name might be a feminine form of the patronymic . In later material appearing in the published version of The Silmarillion, her Adûnaic name was changed to Zimraphel. This final version of the name is inconsistent with the phonetic rules laid out by Tolkien in Lowdham’s Report, which said that the vowels and could only be long in Adûnaic (SD/423).

descriptionText:
The son of Ar- and the 21st ruler of Numenor, whose Quenya name was Tar- *Many-jewels (UT/222). The first element jewel of his Adunaic name seems to have the same meaning as the last element -mir of his Quenya name. The first element MQ. of his Quenya name means a large number, and this might be the meaning of the last element -thon of his Adunaic name, as suggested by Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynn (/23).

Andreas Moehn instead suggested (/ZIMR) that the final element may be the same as the final element of and that the entire name is an of an unattested verb *zimratha- gather jewels. This makes the literal meaning *Jewel-gatherer, which fits if you assume (as Mr. Moehn suggested) that the initial element of Quenya name is actually the verb Q. to gather so that = *Gather-jewels.

A noun translated female and fully declined as an example of an (archaic) feminine Strong II noun (SD/437). The archaic form of this word is zini which is a Strong II noun since it ends in a single short vowel. Its non-archaic form is zini, which is presumably declined as a Weak II noun; most masculine and feminine nouns became weak in Classical Adunaic (SD/436).

A Primitive Adunaic root glossed love, desire, the basis for the verbal element of similar meaning and the noun yearning (SD/423). It is likely also the basis for the noun sweetheart, beloved (SD/424).

An Adunaic verb appearing as an element in various compounds as -zir or zir- (SD/389, 423). The verb was not translated, but its primitive root form is glossed love, desire, so this verb probably has a similar meaning.

Several authors have suggested (/ZIR, /20) that the verb stem is zir- with a short vowel. However, the vowel is long in the participle form beloved, and there are tentative examples where a verb with a short vowel would retain that short vowel in the agental/participle form: *builder. I therefore think that the verb stem is likelier to be zir-.

Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne suggested (/25) that it may be related to the Middle-Period Elvish root M.

An adjective translated (the) beloved (SD/247), apparently formed from the verb to love, desire with the participle suffix . Its placement in the sentence Numenor beloved fell (down) is unusual, since according to Tolkien adjectives normally precede the nouns they modify (SD/428). It is possible that the adjective here is being used as a noun the beloved, an idea supported by the translation of this sentence in the final manuscript: Anadune the beloved she fell (VT24/12). See the entry for the Adunaic for further discussion.

An element in the names and . Imrazor is difficult to translate, but Gimilzor is equated to two different Quenya names at different periods of Tolkiens writing: Star-foam in the unfinished Notion Club Papers story from 1946 (SD/380), and in the list of Adunaic kings in The Lord of the Rings (LotR/1035). The name Telemnar is unglossed, but a likely translation would be *Silver-fire. Assuming the element zor has the same meaning as its Quenya equivalents, could mean either foam or fire. There is a different Adunaic word for foam: or roth in Foam-flower, so perhaps fire is a more useful interpretation, albeit quite speculative.

A noun translated nurse and fully declined as an example of a feminine Weak II noun (SD/438). It has two attested objective forms, an archaic form zoriyu using the ordinary objective inflection and non-archaic form zori, no doubt using the objective inflection -i- often used in feminine nouns (SD/432): zori + -i = zori.
A Primitive Adunaic root glossed one, alone (SD/432), likely the basis for God (the One) and probably related to the Primitive Elvish root of the same meaning.

one ring to bring them all and in the darkness bind them

one ring to rule them all
to bring by force, to hale, to drag
Uglúk to the cesspool, sha! the dungfilth, the great Saruman-fool, skai; Uglúk to torture chamber with stinking Saruman-filth, dung-heap, skai

englishWord: Shadow of the East, Black Easterling

descriptionText: The name by which the first chief of Beorians was known, meaning “Vassal” in the language of his people (S/142). His true name was .
conceptualDevelopment: The name (ᴱN.?) first appeared in the Lays of Beleriand from the 1920s (LB/187). The name remained N. in Silmarillion drafts from the 1930s (LR/274) and was explicitly marked Noldorin in The Etymologies, where it was simply “follower, vassal” used as a name (Ety/BEW). The name fit poorly even with the phonology of the earlier Noldorin language (as discussed in the entry for ), and so in later writings Tolkien reconceived the name as being in the Bëorian language (WJ/218).

descriptionText: Probably deliberately similar to Gnome @@@
The grave of .
Wife of , second known lord of the Hadorians. The elements in her name resemble Adunaic words, which makes sense since Adunaic is descended from the Hadorian language.

The Ilkorin word for father derived from primitive Matar[a], also attested in its plural form edrin (Ety/ATA). It is identical to its Noldorin cognate N. having undergone similar phonetic changes from its primitive form, possibly *atara.

A diminutive form of father, similar to English daddy (Ety/ATA). Helge Fauskanger suggested it may have developed from primitive *atto based on its Quenya equivalent MQ. (AL-Ilkorin/adda), but I think that is likelier to be a childs invention, unrelated to other languages.

A Doriathrin word for bridge appearing in the Addenda and Corrigenda to The Etymologies (EtyAC/YAT), likely a derivative of the same primitive form M as its cognates in other languages. An earlier deleted form iaum may indicate Tolkiens uncertainty over the development of initial [j] (= y) in Ilkorin; elsewhere the rule is that .
An Ilkorin word for swan derived from primitive M (Ety/ALAK). This word is a good example of how in Ilkorin.
Ilkorin for mother (Ety/AM1), also appearing in its plural form emnin (EtyAC/AM1).
An Ilkorin prefix meaning outside, beside, the same as in Quenya and Noldorin (Ety/AR2).

A Doriathrin noun meaning the exterior, the outside, literally outside the fence (Ety/GAT(H)). It is a combination of outside and fence. The entry in The Etymologies also had a rejected variant argadon (EtyAC/GAT(H)).
A name for Doriath translated Outside the Fence, a compound of outside the fence (Ety/AT(AT)) and land (Ety/GAT(H), AR2). Thus, its literal meaning is [Land] Outside the Fence.

A variant form of “[Land] Outside the Fence”, marked as in The Etymologies (Ety/GAT(H), Ety/AR²). If so, it is evidence that in that dialect, primitive [g] became [i] between an [r] and a vowel, just as in the main Ilkorin dialect .
conceptualDevelopment: In the Gnomish Lexicon from the 1910s, ᴱIlk. or Ariador was also said to be a dialectical word, from (early) Ilkorin (GL/20), possibly with a similar phonetic development.

descriptionText: A Doriathrin adjective meaning red derived from the root M (Ety/YAR), likely derived from a primitive form such as *yarna [jarna]. It is a good example of how in Ilkorin.
An adjective meaning violent, rushing, impetuous, appearing as the river name (Ety/SKAR).
A noun meaning cooked food, meat (Ety/AP). Given its Quenya cognate MQ. , it seems to be an example of how voiceless stops became [s] before [s] in Ilkorin.
A suffix, identical to N. (PE21/57). It is possible this suffix was also used as (and was perhaps inspired by) the Gnomish general plural suffix .

A title in The Etymologies translated Vala-king, a combination of the root M and Ilk. king, also attested in its plural form Balthorin (Ety/BAL). It is an example of how voiceless stops became spirants after liquids l and r.
A noun meaning something like home attested only in compounds like Elvenhome.

This word is marked Ilk. in one entry in The Etymologies (Ety/KOR), but elsewhere the same word is marked as Noldorin: N. (Ety/MBAS). The elements of this word are also marked as Noldorin: N. bread (Ety/MBAS) and N. round (Ety/KOR). It is possible the Ilkorin word underwent the same phonetic development as its Noldorin counterpart, or that it is a loan word from Noldorin.
An Ilkorin word for strength, developed from primitive M (Ety/BEL), an example of how final vowels vanished in Ilkorin.
A noun meaning husband developed from primitive M (Ety/BES), the only example of how in Ilkorin.
A noun meaning valiant man, warrior developed from primitive M (Ety/BER) after the primitive final vowel vanished in Ilkorin.
A rejected noun meaning valor developed from the root M (Ety/BER), perhaps from a primitive form *berette. The word was probably rejected when Elbereth change from an Ilkorin to a Noldorin name.

A word meaning steadfast, trusty man, faithful vassal developed from the primitive form Mboron- (Ety/BOR). Because the initial syllable was stressed in the primitive form, the initial [bor-] did not reduce to [br-] as it did when the primitive vowel was unstressed. The glosses seem to indicate that it could be used as an adjective steadfast or a noun trusty man, faithful vassal. However, it is possible that the first part of the gloss is meant to read steadfast/trusty man, so that the word is only a noun.

A word for mast developed from the primitive form M or *beretha (Ety/BERETH), because in Ilkorin . It seems this word referred to beech nuts rather than the mast of a ship, perhaps generalized to all kinds of forest nuts, as in the Old English word mst. The normal Ilkorin word for beech tree is or .
A word for broken stones, gravel developed from the primitive form M or *biritte (Ety/BIRIT), because in Ilkorin .

A word for bear developed from the primitive form M (Ety/BIRIT), because in Ilkorin , after which the . This word is unusual in that the primitive final vowel did not vanish, but instead developed into -a, as noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/broga). The conditions for this exception are unclear, but may have been due to the consonant [g] that developed from primitive [k].

An adjective meaning bowed, bow-shaped, bent developed from the primitive form M (Ety/KU). The middle diphthong went through various sound changes as indicated in The Etymologies. First the [u] became [o] preceding the final [a] (kogna), then the [g] (from ) vocalized to [u] before the [n] (coun) and finally the diphthong [ou] became [au] (caun).
A noun meaning “river” developed from the primitive form ᴹ✶ (Ety/KEL), where the .
conceptualDevelopment: This word was initially marked as Noldorin.

descriptionText: A noun for ship used to in some linguistic notes in the mid-1930s to illustrate the : ciriath. Tolkien first wrote these forms with a short vowel (cir, ciriath), and he vacillated on whether these were Noldorin or Ilkorin words, eventually deciding they were from both languages (PE21/57 noted #28). The proper etymology of the Ilkorin form is unclear; based on the example of < *gwenya we might expect Ilk. **cere instead.

A noun meaning “sickness” (Ety/KWAM). Its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. indicates a primitive form *✶kwāmē, so this word is an example of how initial [kwo] became [ko] after the primitive vowel [ā] became [ō]. Both these developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/côm).
conceptualDevelopment: This word is nearly identical to earlier Gnomish “disease, illness” before Tolkien revised the phonological history of the Noldorin language so that [kw] became [p].

descriptionText: A noun meaning small gull, petrel, sea-bird derived from primitive M (EtyAC/KW, PE22/32), an example of how primitive in Ilkorin. In the Etymologies, this word was marked as Ilkorin (EtyAC/KW), while in Tolkiens description of the Feanorian Alphabet, it was marked as Falathrin (PE22/32).
A Doriathrin noun meaning “Elf” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (EtyAC/KWEN(ED)), an example of the Ilkorin syncope.
conceptualDevelopment: This word is nearly identical to earlier Gnomish “Elf” before Tolkien revised the phonological history of the Noldorin language so that [kw] became [p].

descriptionText: A noun meaning down (feathers) derived from primitive M (Ety/KWES) when the primitive final vowel was lost.

A Doriathrin noun meaning narrator derived from primitive M (Ety/KWET). This word underwent several notable phonetic changes: first the voiceless stop was voiced after the nasal ([nt] > [nd]), after which [e] became [i] before the [nd] ([end] > [ind]) and finally an [o] developed between the consonant and the final [r] ([-dr] > [-dor]). These changes were all noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/cwindor).

A noun meaning shadow of trees, derived from root M shadow and marked as identical in both the Ilkorin and Doriathrin dialects (Ety/DAY). Its primitive form was probably *dair- ending in some final vowel, now lost; Helge Fauskanger suggested it might be *daire (AL-Ilkorin/dair, AL-Doriathrin/dair).

A noun meaning night-time, gloom, derived from root M (Ety/DO). The development of its Noldorin and Quenya cognates point to a primitive form of M [dome] (Ety/DO, DOMO). This word probably underwent development similar to its Noldorin cognate N. but with the retention of the final [-m]: dome > dogme > doume > Ilk. daum. The word Ilk. has an attested development that also follows this pattern (Ety/KU). Helge Fauskanger suggested this same phonological history in his study of Ilkorin (Al-Ilkorin/daum).
Doriathrin name for the leader of the Danians (LR/188), called in their own language Dan. (Ety/DAN). This name developed from the primitive form ᴹ✶.
conceptualDevelopment: In Silmarillion drafts from the 1930s, this name first appeared in forms resembling the Doriathrin name: Denilos or Denithor (SM/271). Later in these drafts, it was change to its Danian form Denethor (LR/119, 145). It kept that form thereafter.

descriptionText: A noun that, together with its variant dang, was glossed sound (Ety/DING). Given that its root form M was said to be onomatopoeic, it was probably a word for a particular kind of sound, perhaps like English twang, which is a gloss of several derivatives of the similar root M.

An Ilkorin noun for head attested only as an element in the name Wet Head (Ety/MIZD, NDOL). It might also appear in , assuming that name is Ilkorin. Assuming it functions similarly to its Noldorin equivalent N. , it can probably also be used to refer to a hill.
A noun glossed flat, lowlying vale (Ety/DAL). Helge Fauskanger pointed out that the gloss is ambiguous, and it may be that this word can also be used an adjective flat (AL-Ilkorin/dol).

A Doriathrin word for back explicitly marked as a noun (Ety/NDAN). Its primitive form might have been *ndan, so that the primitive long [a] became [o] and the initial nasal [n] was lost before the stop (as suggested by Helge Fauskanger, AL-Doriathrin/don).
A Doriathrin noun for land (EtyAC/NDOR) apparently from primitive M (Ety/NDOR). If its primitive form indeed had a short [o], then this word may be an example of how in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin noun meaning oak derived from the primitive form Mdoron[o] (Ety/DORON). The accent mark in the root indicated that the first syllable was stressed, thereby preventing the initial [dor-] from becoming [dr-]. The second [o] was lost, however, due to the Ilkorin syncope.

A Doriathrin noun meaning wolf derived from the primitive form M (Ety/DARAK), probably from older *daraka. The accent mark in the root MDARAK indicated that the first syllable was unstressed, so that the initial [dar-] became [dr-]. Thereafter the long [a], became [o] and the voiceless stop [k] voiced to [g] after the vowel.
A noun meaning river, simply an elaboration of its root M (Ety/DUI).
A noun meaning water, river, simply an elaboration of its root M (Ety/DUI).
A noun for twilight developed from primitive M (Ety/DOMO), where the long .

A Doriathrin adjective meaning black (Ety/DUN). Its Noldorin and Danian cognates imply development from a primitive form *dunna. Since the primitive form ended in [a], the Ilkorin a-affection would ordinarily have produced **donn. However, it seems that a-affection was prevented or reversed before [nn], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/dunn).

A Doriathrin noun for “sorcery” (Ety/ÑGOL). The elements of this word seem to be a combination of derivatives of the roots ᴹ√ and ᴹ√. If it were derived from such a primitive form, it would imply that in its phonological history the [o] because [u] in both syllables. This does not seem to be a general rule in Ilkorin, however: compare Ilk. and . A simpler explanation would be that it was a loan word from Noldorin: N. seen in a marginal note (EtyAC/ÑGOL).
conceptualDevelopment: There is a rejected form dûghol in this entry of The Etymologies that may represent Tolkien’s first attempt to formulate a native Ilkorin word for “sorcery” (EtyAC/ÑGOL). Similar forms appear among the precursors to S. in Lord of the Rings drafts from the 1940s: Dol Dúgol or (TI/178; WR/122). The entry also has a deleted variant form of gûl of Ilk. , so it may be Tolkien originally envisioned a different phonological history of [o] in Ilkorin allowing the production of words like durgul. Perhaps he added the Noldorin form durgul in the margin because he abandoned [o] > [u] in Ilkorin.

descriptionText: The Ilkorin name of MQ. , developed from the same primitive form M (EtyAC/EZDE).
A Doriathrin noun meaning star, a simple derivative of the root M (Ety/EL).

A rejected Doriathrin word for Elf, a derivation of the root M and a direct cognate of MQ. , also appearing in its plural form Eldin (Ety/ELED). It was replaced by Ilk. derived from the inverted form of the root: Medel[a].

An adjectival suffix appearing as both -en and -in, and in one place as -on: . The -en form can be easily explained as a derivative of the primitive suffix M, with the primitive [i] becoming [e] due to Ilkorin a-affection, the same origin as the Noldorin adjectival suffix . The -in variant is more difficult to explain. At least one example had variations with both -en and -in, so perhaps the two forms represented vacillation on the function of Ilkorin a-affection, or an alternate primitive form M-ina where the final a was lost before a-affection.

Alternately, -in could be a Doriathrin-specific variant, since the forms where it appears are all Doriathrin, while the forms where -en appear are marked Ilkorin, excepting only lomen which was itself revised from lomin.
The Ilkorin word for one attested only in the name or Ermab(r)in One-handed (Ety/MAP).
A noun meaning seed, germ derived from primitive M (Ety/ERED). The middle [e] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope, and afterwards the , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/erdh).

A noun meaning sedge derived from the root M (Ety/ESEK), probably from a primitive form *eseke. The middle [e] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope, and afterwards the , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/esg).

A rejected noun meaning rustle, noise of leaves derived from the root M (Ety/EZGE). Its (rejected) Quenya cognate MQ. indicates a primitive form *eseke, despite the root form. If so, middle [e] was lost due to the Ilkorin syncope, and afterwards the .
A noun for wound derived from the root M (Ety/SKAR). Apparently the initial [sk-] became syllabic [sk-], which then became [esk-]. Afterwards the .

A noun for reed-bed, apparently an elaboration of Ilk. reed (Ety/ESEK). In a hastily written entry in The Etymologies, a similar form esgar was glossed shore as a derivative of the root M, but with no language specified (EtyAC/SKAR2). If it was Ilkorin, it probably underwent the same development as wound. Both these words appeared to have been coined to explain the name of the town from the Hobbit.

A noun derived from the root MSPALAS and glossed foaming (?fall); the second word in the gloss is unclear (Ety/PHAL). It was marked as Ilkorin (EtyAC/PHAL). Apparently the initial [sp-] became syllabic [sp-] and then became [esp-].

A Doriathrin noun meaning fence derived from the root M (Ety/GAT(H)), most likely from a primitive form *gat-. As pointed out by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/gad), its gloss is a bit peculiar, given that the other derivatives of its root same to have meanings associated with caves. As Mr. Fauskanger suggested, this may represent a transition in Tolkiens thinking on the meaning of the associated name : Land of the Cave (Ety/GAT(H)) >> Land of the Fence (WJ/370).

A Doriathrin (and Falathrin) noun for beech (tree), a combination of tree and (beech) mast (Ety/GALAD, BERETH). The second element originally meant beech, but later meant mast; this original meaning seems to be preserved in this compound.

A Doriathrin noun for tree derived from the root MGALAD (Ety/GALAD), probably from a primitive form *galada with the second a lost due to the Ilkorin Syncope. Note that the first element [gal-] did not reduce to [gl-] because the initial syllable was stressed in the primitive word.

A noun meaning harp derived from the root M (Ety/NGAN), probably from a primitive form *ngandelle based on its Quenya cognate MQ. . Its plural form genglin is a good representation of the rules for in Ilkorin: the suffix , the syncope of the final vowel and mutation of other vowels. It is also an example of how primitive [nd] sometimes became [g] in Ilkorin. As suggested by Helge Fauskanger, this may be due to assimilation to the preceding [g] (AL-Ilkorin/gangel).

A Doriathrin word (noun and adjective?) for a male derived from the root M (Ety/AN).

Possible Etymology: Its Quenya cognate MQ. indicates a primitive form *anu [anu], but ordinarily a primitive final vowel was lost in Ilkorin. Helge Fauskanger suggested that this Ilkorin word was instead derived for adjective form *anwa [anwa], which would have produced final -u after the loss of the [-a] because final [w] became [u]. This derivation is indicated in the Phonetic Developments given below.

An alternate possibility, though, is that [u] was an exception to the rule that final vowels were lost in Ilkorin. The Noldorin development MAN > ON. > N. hints at a similar process. This uncertainly in its etymology makes it difficult to determine the part of speech (noun and/or adjective) that this word belongs to.

A Doriathrin noun for “wolf” derived from the root ᴹ√ÑGAR(A)M (Ety/ÑGARAM), probably from a primitive form *✶ŋgaramō given its Quenya and Noldorin cognates ᴹQ. and N. (as suggested by Helge Fauskanger, AL-Doriathrin/garm). If so, the second a was lost due to the Ilkorin Syncope, and the the initial [ŋg-] simplified to [g-]. The initial syllable of the primitive form was probably stressed, since the initial [ŋgar-] did not simplify to [ŋgr-].
conceptualDevelopment: An earlier version of this entry had the root ᴹ√ƷARAM, but this produced the same form Dor. garm in Doriathrin [Ilkorin] since initial [ɣ] became [g].

descriptionText: A Doriathrin noun for “lord” derived from the root ᴹ√ or possibly ᴹ√GAR (Ety/ƷAR), perhaps from a primitive form *✶ɣarān-. If so, the initial [ɣ] became [g], while the long [ā] became [ō] and then shortened to [o] in the final syllable of a polysyllable.
conceptualDevelopment: An earlier version of this entry had Dor. garan, which likely had a short [a] in the second syllable which was preserved. Since it did not undergo the Ilkorin Syncope, the primitive form likely either had no final vowel or ended in a short [a], so the second [a] was in the final syllable, which seems to have prevented the syncope; this theory is supported by its Quenya cognate ᴹQ. .

descriptionText: An adjective meaning bright derived from the root M, the basis of the river name (Ety/GYEL). There isnt enough information to deduce its primitive form, but Helge Fauskanger suggested *galjana (AL-Ilkorin/gelion), which seems reasonably plausible.
A Doriathrin noun for sky derived from the root M (Ety/EL), probably from a primitive form *elle [elle] based on its cognates. It is a clear example of how initial [] became [g] in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin adjective meaning (pale) blue derived from the root M (Ety/EL), probably from a primitive form *elwa [elwa] based on its cognates. If so, the initial [] became [g], the primitive final [a] vanished, after which the final [w] became [u]. These developments were noted by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/gelu).

A preposition “from, away” marked as both Ilkorin (Ety/ƷŌ̆; PE21/60) and Doriathrin (EtyAC/ƷŌ̆). It developed from primitive ᴹ✶ʒō̆ (Ety/WŌ), with the initial [ɣ] becoming [g]. It was also used as patronymic, as in go-Thingol “*child of Thingol” (Ety/ƷŌ̆).
conceptualDevelopment: This preposition may be a restoration of the Gnomish patronymic G. .

descriptionText: A noun meaning dirtiness, filth derived from primitive M (Ety/WA). This word underwent quite a few phonetic developments, as indicated below and as described by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/god).

A verb meaning to soil, stain derived from primitive M (Ety/WA). This word underwent quite a few phonetic developments similar to those of related dirtiness, filth, as indicated below and as described by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/goda-).

A (rejected?) Doriathrin noun for light derived from primitive M appearing in The Etymologies (Ety/KAL, EtyAC/KAL). According to Christopher Tolkiens notes, it was part of a rejected etymology for the name , but it isnt clear whether this noun was rejected or if it was just the etymology. Its long primitive vowel [a] became [o] as was the norm in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin name for the Silmarils, a combination of the genitive form of Noldo and jewel (Ety/MIR, NGOLOD), hence: *Noldo-jewel. It also appeared in the variant form Goldomir, which may hint at the primitive form of the .

An adjective meaning soiled, dirty derived from primitive M [wara] (Ety/WA). This word underwent quite a few phonetic developments, as indicated below and as described by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gor).

A noun glossed shade (shadow) derived from the root M (Ety/WATH). It is a clear example of how in Ilkorin, and it appears in several names: (Woman of) Secret Shadow and (unglossed but presumably *Mountains of Shadow).
A noun meaning wind derived from the root MWAW(A) (Ety/WA). Here the , and after the final vowel vanished, the final [w] became [u].
A noun meaning bond derived from primitive M (Ety/WED). Here the , and the [d] spirantalized to [].

A noun for “air” or “the lower air”, derived from the same primitive form ᴹ✶ as its Quenya equivalent ᴹQ. Wilwa (Ety/WIL). Here the . Furthermore, after the final [a] was lost, the final [w] became [u] and then became [o], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gwelo).
conceptualDevelopment: In the Addenda and Corrigenda to The Etymologies, Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne indicated the Tolkien revised this form to gwelm at the same time as he change its primitive to ᴹ✶wilmā and the Quenya form to ᴹQ. Wilma (EtyAC/WIL). This entry keeps the earlier Ilkorin form gwelo because Tolkien never revised ᴹQ. Wilwa in the narratives of this period.

descriptionText: A noun for girl derived from primitive M (Ety/WEN). Here the .
A noun for greenness derived from the root M (Ety/GWEN).

An adjective for green derived from the root M (Ety/GWEN). Its Quenya cognate MQ. wenya suggests its primitive form was *gwenya [gwenja]. If so, it is an example of how, after final [a] was lost, the final [j] became [i] and then became [e], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/gwene).

A noun for butterfly derived from the root M (Ety/GWEN). Its Quenya cognate MQ. wilwarind- suggests its primitive form was *wilwarinde. If so, it is an example of how [nd] sometimes became [g] in Ilkorin. As suggested by Helge Fauskanger, this may be due to assimilation to the preceding [g] (AL-Ilkorin/gwilwering).
An adjective for pale blue derived from the root MGWINDI, rejected along with its root (EtyAC/GWINDI).

A noun for evening derived from primitive Mwinya [winja], but it was rejected along with its root MWIN (Ety/WIN). It is the clearest example of the Ilkorin phonetic development whereby final [j] became [i] and then became [e], since Tolkien indicated the intermediate forms before rejecting the word.
A noun for spindrift, flying spray derived from primitive M (Ety/WIG). Here the .

An archaic prefix meaning together derived from primitive M (Ety/WO). It was lost because it coalesced with the preposition from. As such, it is the clearest example of how initial [gwo] became [go] in Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin adjective for grey written heu in The Etymologies, and derived from the primitive form M [khithwa] (Ety/KHIS). This word illustrates several interesting phonetic changes in Ilkorin.

  1. The [i] became [e] before the final [a].
  2. Both the : [kh-] > [x-] and [-th-] > [--].
    1. Later the .
    2. Meanwhile the medial [--] voiced to [--] (dh).
  3. The primitive final [a] was lost.
  4. Afterwards, the resulting final [w] became [u].

In most other Doriathrin words, a final [u] from [w] further developed into [o]; it is unclear why this change did not occur here.
A noun glossed captain derived from the root M command (EtyAC/KHES). The language of this word is unclear; Carl Hostetter and Patrick Wynne indicated it might be ?Bel. for Beleriandic = Ilkorin.

A Doriathrin noun for fog written hium in The Etymologies, and derived from the primitive form M [khithme] (Ety/KHIS, EtyAC/KHIS). This word illustrates several interesting phonetic changes in Ilkorin.

  1. Both the : [kh-] > [x-] and [-th-] > [--].
    1. Later the .
    2. Meanwhile the medial [--] voiced to [--] (dh).
  2. The primitive final [e] was lost.
  3. Afterwards, the resulting final [m] became syllabic and developed into [-um].
A Doriathrin noun for lady attested only as an element in the name (Ety/NEL). It probably had essentially the same derivation as its Noldorin cognate N. (Ety/KHER).
A word for a blow with an axe in Early Noldorin Word-lists of the 1920s derived from primitive Eskanta (PE13/147).
Apparently a feminine suffix attested only in the name (Ety/LUK).
Apparently a feminine suffix attested in the name (Woman of) Secret Shadow (Ety/THUR) and the noun queen (Ety/TA).
A suffix appearing in almost all attested Ilkorin plurals.
conceptualDevelopment: This suffix is the same as the most common Gnomish plural suffix (GG/10).

descriptionText: The Doriathrin word for the Moon developed from the primitive name M (Ety/I2), though it is unclear how the [st] developed. Perhap it was of the same origin as silver light, starlight (Ety/SIL).

A Doriathrin noun for silver light, starlight, also given as istel, which developed from the root M (Ety/SIL). Tolkien said that it was probably originally a (ancient?) Quenya word learned from Melian. This apparently this means its development was unusual. Along with the identical Moon, it is the only Ilkorin noun with a medial [st]. Helge Fauskanger suggested it must have developed by a strengthening of [s] to [st]. It may also be another example of a development from syllabic [s], though elsewhere .
A rejected Doriathrin noun for babe developed from the root M (EtyAC/LAP). Its Quenya cognate MQ. suggests a primitive form of *lapse, but elsewhere a medial [ps] became [ss] in Ilkorin, as with < M.

An adjective meaning fresh, lively developed from the primitive form M (Ety/LAYAK). It is a good example of how in Ilkorin, as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/laig). This allowed it to blend with the derivative of M and assume the additional meanings keen, sharp (Ety/LAIK).

A noun meaning elm-tree developed from the root M (Ety/ALAM). An identical form appeared elsewhere in The Etymologies with its language marked D, perhaps for Doriathrin (Ety/LALAM). This word is unusual in that its final [m] did not become syllabic after a consonant, although it did for other similar words such as .

englishWord: licking up (food or drink), gluttonous eating

descriptionText: A Doriathrin noun for gold developed from primitive M, properly golden light rather than the metal (Ety/LAWAR).

An adjective meaning tuneful, sweet developed from primitive M (Ety/LIND, EtyAC/LIND). It is an example of how the usual Ilkorin a-affection was prevented or reverted before [nd], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/lind). This word may also have had the sense *singing in the word nightingale = *night singing, from primitive M.

A noun for pool derived from the root M (Ety/LIN1). Its Quenya cognate MQ. suggests its primitive form was *linya [linja]. If so, it is an example of how, after final [a] was lost, the final [j] became [i] and then became [e], as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Ilkorin/line).
A Doriathrin noun for “fish” derived from primitive ᴹ✶ (Ety/LIW). It is the clearest example of how , as suggested by Helge Fauskanger (AL-Doriathrin/líw). @@@ same development in ᴱN hiw PE13/147
conceptualDevelopment: This word first appeared as rejected ling (EtyAC/LIW), probably reflecting Tolkien’s uncertainty on the development of [-ŋgw-] in Ilkorin.
